## [2026-05-24] ingest | DSPy Tutorial — Image Generation Prompt Iteration (dspy.Image + Flux Pro via FAL)

- **Source**: `https://dspy.ai/tutorials/image_generation_prompting/` (saved to `raw/dspy-tutorials/image-generation-prompting.md`) — official [[DSPy]] tutorial. **Twentieth wiki-corpus DSPy tutorial** and the **first wiki receipt of an image modality in DSPy**. Author credit: *"based off of a tweet from @ThorondorLLC"*.
- **Files created**: `raw/dspy-tutorials/image-generation-prompting.md`, `wiki/sources/dspy-image-generation-prompting-tutorial.md`, `wiki/concepts/DSPyImage.md`, `wiki/concepts/FluxPro.md`, `wiki/concepts/GPT4oMini.md`, `wiki/concepts/IterativeImagePromptRefinement.md`, `wiki/entities/FAL.md`, `wiki/entities/BlackForestLabs.md`.
- **Files updated**: `wiki/index.md` (1 source under DSPy Tutorial cluster adjacent to [[dspy-tutorial-games]] / [[dspy-yahoo-finance-react-tutorial]]; 4 concepts — DSPyImage + IterativeImagePromptRefinement adjacent to [[DSPyAudio]] in the DSPy-primitives cluster, GPT4oMini adjacent to [[GPT4oMiniAudio]] in the OpenAI-models cluster, FluxPro adjacent to [[DiffusionModel]] in the image-generation cluster; 2 entities — FAL adjacent to [[FastMCP]] in the F cluster, BlackForestLabs adjacent to [[BespokeLabsAI|Bespoke Labs]] in the B cluster); `wiki/overview.md` (new Update block at top); `wiki/log.md` (this entry).
- **Headline contribution**: opens the **image modality** axis in DSPy alongside the existing audio coverage ([[dspy-audio-tutorial]]). Establishes that DSPy's two non-text primitives — `dspy.Image` and `dspy.Audio` — use **opposite transport disciplines** (URL passthrough vs base64 inlining) matched to each modality's common provenance pattern. The wiki's multimodal coverage is now **structurally symmetric** across modalities: input-side first-class via the primitive on a Signature `InputField`, output-side wrapped HTTP outside the DSPy `LM` abstraction inside a manual `forward()`-like loop.
- **Program shape**: a single string-spec [[DSPyPredict|`dspy.Predict`]] (`"desired_prompt: str, current_image: dspy.Image, current_prompt:str -> feedback:str, image_strictly_matches_desired_prompt: bool, revised_prompt: str"`) wrapped in a plain Python `for i in range(max_iter=5)` loop with early break on the boolean match field. **No [[DSPyModules|`dspy.Module`]] subclass**, no [[DSPyOptimization|Optimization stage]], no [[DSPyMetrics|metric]], no eval set. Image generator is [[FluxPro|Flux Pro v1.1 Ultra]] via [[FAL]]; critic is [[GPT4oMini|`gpt-4o-mini`]] at `temperature=0.5`.
- **First wiki receipts within this tutorial**: (1) [[DSPyImage|`dspy.Image`]] primitive on a Signature `InputField`; (2) `dspy.Image.from_url(url)` construction path; (3) **URL-passthrough adapter wire shape** (`<image_url: https://fal.media/files/.../*.jpg>` carried verbatim, no base64 inlining) — opposite transport discipline from [[DSPyAudio|`dspy.Audio`]]'s base64-in-`data` storage; (4) `dspy.Image` named inline in a string-spec Signature — proves the string-Signature parser resolves the `dspy.` namespace prefix as a typed field reference; (5) **string-Signature outputs are field-set-canonical, not field-order-canonical** — `inspect_history(5)` shows different output-field orders across runs (`feedback / revised_prompt / image_strictly_matches_desired_prompt` in run 1 vs `feedback / image_strictly_matches_desired_prompt / revised_prompt` in runs 2–5); (6) [[FluxPro|Flux Pro v1.1 Ultra]] and [[FAL]] as the image-generation provider stack in a DSPy program; (7) `python-dotenv` `load_dotenv()` for credential loading; (8) `temperature=0.5` for a single-Signature critic; (9) two-provider, no-HF-dataset DSPy tutorial shape (OpenAI + FAL, no [[HuggingFace]]); (10) the [[IterativeImagePromptRefinement|critic-then-revise loop pattern]] — natural [[GEPA]] target none of the current GEPA tutorials exercises on the image modality.
- **Tutorial-author honesty**: the tutorial **explicitly disclaims its own optimizability** — *"this is not DSPy prompt optimization as it is normally used, but it is a good example of how to use multimodal DSPy"* — and names the natural lift (*"a future upgrade would be to create a dataset of initial, final prompts to optimize the prompt generation"*). **First DSPy tutorial in the wiki that ships a working program while explicitly disclaiming the Optimizer surface**.
- **Cross-receipt against [[dspy-audio-tutorial]]**: structural symmetry across the two non-text modalities — both are input-first-class (`dspy.Image` / `dspy.Audio` on Signature `InputField`s) and output-wrapped-HTTP (FAL's [[FluxPro|Flux Pro]] HTTP API for image generation; OpenAI's [[GPT4oMiniTTS|TTS]] HTTP API for audio generation, both outside the DSPy `LM` abstraction inside manual wrappers). **Opposite transport disciplines** at the input wire shape — URL passthrough for `dspy.Image`, base64 inlining for `dspy.Audio` — matched to each modality's common provenance.
- **Cross-receipt against [[dspy-tool-use-tutorial]]**: both tutorials use a hand-rolled outer loop instead of a `dspy.Module` subclass, but for different reasons — tool-use uses [[HandRolledReAct]] because [[ToolHop]] ships per-question tools (tools-as-runtime-input); this tutorial uses a plain `for` loop because the program is programming-stage-only with no Optimizer in scope.
- **Cross-receipt against GEPA tutorials** ([[dspy-tutorial-gepa-aime]], [[dspy-tutorial-gepa-facilitysupportanalyzer]], [[dspy-tutorial-gepa-papillon]], [[dspy-tutorial-gepa-trusted-monitor]]): the [[IterativeImagePromptRefinement|critic-then-revise loop]] pattern this tutorial hand-rolls is **structurally what [[GEPA]] automates** (reflective prompt mutation reading natural-language feedback per example and proposing a revised instruction). **The most natural candidate in the DSPy tutorial corpus for a future GEPA receipt on a multimodal task** — none of the existing GEPA tutorials in the wiki exercises the image modality.

## [2026-05-24] ingest | DSPy Tutorial — Classification Fine-tuning (Banking77 via Local Llama-3.2-1B)
- **Source**: `raw/dspy-tutorial-classification-finetuning.ipynb` (Jupyter notebook fetched from `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/main/docs/docs/tutorials/classification_finetuning/index.ipynb`, ~44 KB).
- **Source page**: [[dspy-tutorial-classification-finetuning]].
- **Headline**: **The wiki's first end-to-end runnable receipt of [[BootstrapFinetune|`dspy.BootstrapFinetune`]]** — the only weight-tuning optimizer in [[DSPyOptimizers|the catalog]] — and the **first DSPy tutorial whose output is a fine-tuned local open-weights model** rather than a prompt-optimized program. Two-stage Banking77 distillation: stage A bootstraps from **500 unlabeled** examples (no metric filter) → **51.5%** dev accuracy; stage B bootstraps from **500 labeled** examples with a `lambda x, y, trace=None: x.label == y.label` metric filter → **86.7%** dev accuracy. **Cross-model result**: fine-tuned local [[Llama|Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct]] student (86.7%) **beats** [[GPT|GPT-4o-mini]] teacher (55%) by **+31.7 absolute / +57.6% relative** — *inverted distillation* where the ~50× smaller open-weights student outperforms the API teacher.
- **First wiki receipts within this tutorial**:
  1. End-to-end `dspy.BootstrapFinetune(num_threads=16, metric=...)` invocation with the `metric=` filter; the metric filters teacher rollouts that disagree with the gold label out of the SFT dataset before [[HuggingFaceTRL|TRL SFTTrainer]] sees them.
  2. `dspy.settings.experimental = True` as a hard precondition for weight-space optimization in DSPy.
  3. `dspy.clients.lm_local.LocalProvider()` + `openai/local:<hf-model-id>` model-prefix idiom for [[SGLang]]-backed local serving.
  4. Explicit `.launch()` / `.kill()` lifecycle on the fine-tuned LM between Stage A and Stage B to free GPU memory.
  5. `DSPY_FINETUNEDIR` environment variable as a first-class DSPy knob (with `DSPY_CACHEDIR` fallback) alongside `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES`.
  6. The full `train_kwargs` surface for local-LM fine-tuning: `device`, `use_peft`, `num_train_epochs`, `per_device_train_batch_size`, `gradient_accumulation_steps`, `learning_rate`, `max_seq_length`, `packing`, `bf16`, `output_dir` — passed through to TRL.
  7. The `transformers==4.48.3` version pin justified inline by linking to <https://github.com/huggingface/trl/issues/2338>.
  8. The second wiki receipt of `program.deepcopy()` + `program.set_lm(lm)` (used twice — student and teacher in the same program).
  9. MLflow saving / loading a **weight-tuned** DSPy program via `mlflow.dspy.log_model(classify_ft, artifact_path="model")` + `mlflow.dspy.load_model(...)` (prior MLflow receipts saved only prompt-tuned programs).
- **Second Banking77 BFT receipt** — completes the matrix begun by the [[dspy-optimizers|page 13]] narrative receipt:
  - **Prior receipt** ([[dspy-optimizers]]): API self-distillation (GPT-4o-mini → fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini) with the `text, hint -> label` training-time hint trick on 2000 examples → 66 → 87%.
  - **This tutorial**: cross-model open-weights distillation (GPT-4o-mini teacher → fine-tuned local Llama-3.2-1B student), no hint trick, 500 examples per stage → 51.5 / 55 → 86.7%.
  - **Both converge on ~87% post-BFT within 0.3 points** despite radically different inference and fine-tuning substrates — evidence that BFT's metric-filter mechanism dominates the substrate choice on closed-set classification.
- **Third local-weight-tuning DSPy tutorial** after [[dspy-tutorial-rl-papillon]] and [[dspy-rl-multihop-tutorial]] — fills the **supervised** weight-tuning branch (SFT via [[HuggingFaceTRL|TRL]] + [[HuggingFacePEFT|PEFT]]) alongside the **RL** weight-tuning branch (GRPO via [[Arbor]] + [[lora|LoRA]]) the prior two established. **[[SGLang]] is the common inference substrate**: direct via `LocalProvider` here, indirect via Arbor in the GRPO tutorials.
- **Cross-receipt with [[KnowledgeDistillation|knowledge distillation]]**: first wiki receipt where the student **strictly outperforms** the teacher on the target distribution rather than compressing it with quality loss. The teacher's *traces* (reasoning + answer) plus a metric filter exceed the teacher's *direct accuracy* — concrete measurement of bootstrap-distillation's amplification effect on Banking77.
- **Twenty-ninth wiki-corpus DSPy tutorial**.
- **New pages minted**: 2 entity pages — [[Banking77]] (77-way intent classification dataset from [[PolyAI]]; the canonical fine-grained intent-classification benchmark in the DSPy corpus), [[PolyAI]] (publisher of Banking77, [[HuggingFace]] dataset `PolyAI/banking77`).
- **Updated in place**: [[BootstrapFinetune]] (second runnable receipt + cross-architecture reconciliation table), [[DSPyOptimizers]] (third optimizer-family end-to-end receipt), [[DSPyLM]] (`LocalProvider` + `openai/local:` prefix surface), [[SGLang]] (first DSPy-fine-tuning receipt), [[HuggingFaceTRL]] / [[HuggingFacePEFT]] (passthrough train_kwargs surface from DSPy), [[Llama]] (Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct DSPy student receipt) / [[meta]], [[KnowledgeDistillation]] (student-beats-teacher inverted-distillation receipt), [[chainofthought]] (`Literal{CLASSES}` inline-string-form closed-set output receipt), [[MLflow]] (first save/load of a weight-tuned DSPy program), [[Ollama]] (named as future fine-tuned-model inference substrate), [[Classification]], [[FineTuning]], [[SupervisedFinetuning]] sources frontmatter in place.
- **Contradictions**: none with the existing wiki. Result reinforces the [[BootstrapFinetune]] page's *21-point lift* claim by extending the BFT envelope to **+32 points** (student post-Stage-B vs teacher baseline) on the same dataset with a different student architecture. Inverts the typical [[KnowledgeDistillation]] direction — first concrete measurement in the wiki.
- **Scope-limit gaps**: no cost / wall-time / VRAM disclosure; no `train_kwargs` sweep; no `use_peft=True` / LoRA ablation (headline 86.7% is full-parameter SFT); no MIPROv2-vs-BFT head-to-head on the same task; no `BetterTogether` composition; no multi-seed variance; no alternative student / teacher pairing; no SFT-dataset-composition analysis; no checkpoint resumption (Stage B re-trains from `student_lm` from scratch); no plain `program.save/load` for the fine-tuned program (only MLflow path shown); no [[Ollama]] deployment (explicitly flagged as future work).

## [2026-05-24] ingest | DSPy Tutorial — GEPA for Facility Support Analyzer (Structured Information Extraction)
- **Source**: `raw/dspy-tutorial-gepa-facility-support-analyzer.md` (markdown fetched from `https://dspy.ai/tutorials/gepa_facilitysupportanalyzer/index.md`, 343 KB / 3360 lines).
- **Source page**: [[dspy-tutorial-gepa-facility-support-analyzer]].
- **Headline**: **Second wiki-corpus end-to-end runnable `dspy.GEPA` receipt** after [[dspy-tutorial-gepa-aime]] — extends the GEPA envelope from **single-Signature math reasoning** to **three-Signature enterprise classification** over the Meta-released [[FacilitySupportAnalyzer]] dataset (200 ProCare facility-support emails). Three sibling [[chainofthought|`dspy.ChainOfThought`]] predictors inside `FacilitySupportAnalyzerMM`: urgency (3-way `Literal`), sentiment (3-way `Literal`), categories (10-way `List[Literal[...]]` multi-label). **Asymmetric two-model pair**: [[GPT|GPT-4.1 nano]] student (`openai/gpt-4.1-nano`, `temperature=1`) reflected on by [[GPT|GPT-5]] (`temperature=1.0`, `max_tokens=32000`). Configuration: `dspy.GEPA(metric=metric_with_feedback, auto="light", num_threads=32, track_stats=True, use_merge=False, reflection_lm=...)`. Train/Val/Test = 66/66/68 (shuffled with `random.Random(0)`). **Lift: 75.4% → 87.0%** (51.30 → 59.17 on 68-item test set) — clean +11.6 absolute points at `auto="light"`. Closing line: *"GEPA was able to optimize GPT-4.1 nano's performance from 75% score to 87% in the auto='light' setting."*
- **Three new disclosures to the wiki's GEPA documentation**:
  1. **`use_merge` is an explicit `dspy.GEPA(...)` kwarg** — first wiki receipt of the [[SystemAwareMerge|GEPA+Merge]] toggle as a kwarg name; explicitly `False` here.
  2. **GEPA mutates one predictor per iteration on multi-module programs** — log rotates `urgency_module.predict` (iter 1, 4, 7, ...), `sentiment_module.predict` (iter 2, 5, 8, ...), `categories_module.predict` (iter 3, 6, 9, ...). The reflection LM never asked to rewrite all sibling predictors in one mutation step.
  3. **`pred_name`-routed `metric_with_feedback`** — the canonical multi-module $\mu_f$ pattern: a single function branches on `pred_name in {'urgency_module.predict', 'sentiment_module.predict', 'categories_module.predict'}` to return predictor-specific failure analyses. First wiki receipt of this pattern in [[FeedbackFunction]].
- **Evolved instructions shape**: three orthogonal decision frameworks (one per predictor) rather than one mega-prompt — urgency (safety/risk + operational impact + time sensitivity + tone-vs-intent), sentiment (explicit emotional language vs polite formality + tone dominance), categories (strict evidence + scheduling-vs-complaint disambiguation + specialized-vs-routine cleaning + multi-label assignment). **First wiki receipt of GEPA producing parallel sibling instructions** vs [[dspy-tutorial-gepa-aime|the AIME tutorial]]'s single ~120-line monolithic playbook.
- **Pareto-front receipt**: 9 specialist programs retained alongside aggregate-best program 17 in the printed Graphviz DAG (programs 4, 8, 9, 12, 13, 15, 19, 20, 21). Programs 19 (0.74) and 21 (0.77) sit **below the un-optimized baseline** (0.72) on aggregate yet remain on the per-instance Pareto front — concrete receipt that [[ParetoBasedCandidateSelection|specialist retention]] keeps programs with strictly worse aggregate than baseline.
- **Validation trajectory**: 22 candidate programs (0–21); 86% plateau reached at iter 6 (program 4 at 0.8611); held through 28 intervening iterations; finally cleared by 0.0015 points at iter 35 (program 17 at 0.8626). Test score on optimized program: 0.8701.
- **New surfaces documented**: `detailed_results` attribute (8 fields: `candidates`, `parents`, `val_aggregate_scores`, `val_subscores`, `per_val_instance_best_candidates`, `discovery_eval_counts`, `best_outputs_valset`, `best_idx`, `best_candidate`); `dag_to_dot(...)` Graphviz-DOT trajectory visualization recipe; `find_dominator_programs(...)` from `gepa.gepa_utils`; `display_table=True` on `dspy.Evaluate(...)`; `optimized_program.named_predictors()` iteration for inspecting post-optimization instructions across multiple sub-modules.
- **Three-tutorial GEPA envelope** (AIME / PAPILLON / Facility) now established: same optimizer settings (`auto="light"` or smallest non-zero budget, GPT-5 or GPT-4.1 reflector); varying student LM tier (Mini / Nano / nano), program decomposition (1 / 2 / 3 predictors), feedback topology (dense narrative / per-axis decomposition / `pred_name`-routed), benchmark difficulty (math reasoning / privacy-preserving delegation / enterprise classification). Lifts: +10 / +9.6 / +11.6 absolute points.
- **Contradictions flagged**: none — extends every prior GEPA receipt along orthogonal axes (student tier, predictor count, feedback topology, benchmark family).
- **Scope gaps** (9): no cost disclosure (same break as [[dspy-tutorial-gepa-aime]] + [[dspy-tutorial-gepa-papillon]]); no `auto="medium"`/`"heavy"` comparison despite the explicit recommendation in the inline callout (*"we typically recommend using auto='heavy' for optimized performance!"*); no reflection-LM ablation; no save/load receipt; no MIPROv2-vs-GEPA comparison on the same task; no streaming/async/observability composition; no baseline-prompt printout (only Signature docstrings printed); `use_merge=True` ablation not run; no analysis of why the iter-6 plateau persisted for 29 iterations before program 17 cleared.
- **Validation**: source page exists (`wiki/sources/dspy-tutorial-gepa-facility-support-analyzer.md`); 1 new concept page minted ([[FacilitySupportAnalyzer]]); 4 existing concept pages updated in place ([[GEPA]] with third runnable tutorial receipt + three-tutorial envelope table; [[FeedbackFunction]] with multi-predictor routing section and `pred_name` switch worked example; [[ReflectivePromptMutation]] with multi-module rotation section and parallel sibling artifacts; [[ParetoBasedCandidateSelection]] with specialist-retention receipt and 9-program front DAG). Index entries inserted: 1 source (Sources block, top of GEPA tutorial cluster), 1 concept ([[FacilitySupportAnalyzer]] in Concepts block adjacent to other GEPA primitives). All `[[wikilinks]]` resolve to existing pages.

## [2026-05-24] ingest | DSPy Tutorial — GEPA for AIME (Math)
- **Source**: `raw/dspy-tutorial-gepa-aime.md` (notebook `docs/docs/tutorials/gepa_aime/index.ipynb` from `stanfordnlp/dspy` GitHub repo, fetched via the GitHub Contents API and converted to markdown; canonical web URL `https://dspy.ai/tutorials/gepa_aime/`).
- **Source page**: [[dspy-tutorial-gepa-aime]].
- **Headline**: The **wiki's first runnable end-to-end receipt of [[GEPA|`dspy.GEPA`]]** — the reflection-driven instruction optimizer from [[2507.19457-gepa]]. Optimizes a one-line `dspy.ChainOfThought("problem -> answer")` (one-sentence baseline instruction *"Solve the problem and provide the answer in the correct format."*) on AIME contest math with the canonical asymmetric LM pair ([[GPT|GPT-4.1 Mini]] student at `temperature=1, max_tokens=32000` reflected on by [[GPT|GPT-5]] at `temperature=1.0, max_tokens=32000`), `auto="light"`, `num_threads=32`, `track_stats=True`, `reflection_minibatch_size=3`. **Lift: 46.7% → 56.7% on AIME-2025 ×5** (70 → 85 correct on 150 test items) — clean +10 absolute points at the smallest budget setting. Qualitatively replicates the [[2507.19457-gepa|GEPA paper's]] headline GPT-4.1 Mini × [[AIME2025|AIME-2025]] result (paper Table 1: 45.33 → 59.33 at full budget).

The lift is **load-bearing on training-set quality** in a way scalar-metric optimizers are not.
- **Cross-receipt convergence with [[2507.19457-gepa|the paper]]**: paper Table 1 cell GPT-4.1 Mini × AIME-2025: 45.33 → 59.33 (paper full budget, 30-problem single eval); tutorial: 46.7 → 56.7 (`auto="light"` ≈ 6.22 full evals, 150-eval ×5 oversampling). Pre-3.0.0 explicitly disavows cross-version BC; 3.0.0+ will guarantee BC within major versions.

  - The [[MLflow]] integration ladder (track → trace → store → serve from [[dspy-deployment-tutorial]], now → durable-artifact-primitive from this tutorial) is now end-to-end: this tutorial supplies the underlying `save/load` primitives that the MLflow integration **wraps**.
- **Productive clarifications**:
  1. **Whole-program mode requires DSPy ≥ 2.6.0.** Pre-2.6.0 users must reconstruct the architecture; this is a hard floor, not a soft preference.
  2. **State-only `.json` is the only inspectable mode.** Pickle (state-only) and cloudpickle (whole-program) artifacts are opaque binaries — the inspectability discipline only applies to JSON state-only mode.
  3. **JSON state-only flattens demos to `dict`.** Pickle-mode state-only and whole-program-mode preserve [[DSPyExample|`dspy.Example`]] identity (pickle round-trips Python class identity). The **final chapter of the book** and the **twelfth chapter from *Hands-On LLMs*** (after Chs 1–11) — **the third and last chapter of Part III ("Training and Fine-Tuning Language Models")**; the generative-model counterpart to [[hands-on-llm-ch11-fine-tuning-representation-models|Ch 11]] (representation models) and the runnable-code resolution of [[hands-on-llm-ch01-introduction-to-llms|Ch 1]]'s *"forward-reference Ch 12 for fine-tuning generative models with RLHF / DPO"* promise. **This ingest completes the 12-chapter Hands-On LLMs ingest** — the wiki's **third fully-ingested LLM book** after [[ai-engineering-chip-huyen|*AI Engineering* (Chip Huyen, O'Reilly 2024)]] and [[LLMEngineersHandbook|*LLM Engineer's Handbook* (Iusztin, Labonne & Vesa, Packt 2024)]], alongside [[mml-book|*Mathematics for Machine Learning* (Deisenroth, Faisal & Ong, Cambridge 2020)]] which is in progress.
- **Source page**: [[hands-on-llm-ch12-fine-tuning-generation-models]].
- **Scope**: The **two-stage fine-tuning pipeline for generative LLMs** walked end-to-end on the same base ([[TinyLlama|TinyLlama-1.1B]]) using the Hugging Face stack ([[transformers]] + [[peft|PEFT]] + [[bitsandbytes]] + [[trl|TRL]]). **Stage 1 — [[SupervisedFinetuning|SFT]]** via [[QLoRA]]: 4-bit NF4 quantization (`BitsAndBytesConfig` — `load_in_4bit=True`, `bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4"`, `bnb_4bit_compute_dtype="float16"`, `bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True`) + [[lora|LoRA]] adapter (`LoraConfig` — `r=64`, `α=32`, `lora_dropout=0.1`, `bias="none"`, `task_type="CAUSAL_LM"`, `target_modules=["k_proj","gate_proj","v_proj","up_proj","q_proj","o_proj","down_proj"]` — all 7 Llama-family projection layers) + [[SFTTrainer|`trl.SFTTrainer`]] on 3,000 [[UltraChat]] examples formatted in TinyLlama's `<|user|>...<|assistant|>` [[ChatTemplate]]; `optim="paged_adamw_32bit"`, `lr=2e-4`, `lr_scheduler_type="cosine"`, `num_train_epochs=1`, `fp16=True`, `gradient_checkpointing=True`, `per_device_train_batch_size=2`, `gradient_accumulation_steps=4` (effective batch 8); single-epoch SFT ≈ **1 hour on a free Google Colab Tesla T4**; loaded base uses **~1 GB VRAM** (vs ~4 GB FP16). Merge via [[AutoPeftModelForCausalLM|`peft.AutoPeftModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(...).merge_and_unload()`]] to fuse the LoRA delta back into the 16-bit base. **Stage 2 — [[PreferenceFinetuning|Preference Tuning]]** via [[DPO]]: same QLoRA config applied via [[DPOTrainer|`trl.DPOTrainer`]] + [[DPOConfig|`trl.DPOConfig`]] on `argilla/distilabel-intel-orca-dpo-pairs` (~6,000 filtered triples after `status != "tie"` + `chosen_score >= 8` + `not in_gsm8k_train` filter from ~13,000 raw); `beta=0.1`, `learning_rate=1e-5` (10× lower than SFT — DPO updates destabilize otherwise), `lr_scheduler_type="cosine"`, `max_steps=200`, `warmup_ratio=0.1`, `max_prompt_length=512`, `max_length=512`. **Iterative adapter merging**: merge SFT adapter into base → merge DPO adapter into the SFT-merged model. **PEFT framing**: walks the two named PEFT families — [[adapterlayers|Houlsby 2019 adapters]] (3.6% of BERT params → within 0.4% of full FT on GLUE; AdapterHub + LLaMA-Adapter as extensions) and [[lora|LoRA]] (Hu et al. 2021, justified by [[IntrinsicDimension|intrinsic dimension]] — Aghajanyan, Zettlemoyer & Gupta 2020 arXiv:2012.13255) — anchored in the GPT-3 175B 12,288×12,288 rank-8 → 197K-params-per-block intuition. **QLoRA innovations** (Dettmers et al. 2023, arXiv:2305.14314) walked operationally: [[BlockwiseQuantization|blockwise quantization]] (per-block quantization constants) + [[NormalFloat4|NF4]] (bin original weights by relative density to a normal distribution between –1 and 1) + [[DoubleQuantization|double quantization]] + [[PagedOptimizer|paged optimizers]] ([[PagedAdamW32bit|`paged_adamw_32bit`]]). **Reward-model + [[PPO]] baseline** explained as the algorithm DPO replaces: [[RewardModel|reward model]] = SFT-initialized model with language-modeling head replaced by a scalar quality head; Llama 2's **two-reward-model design** (helpfulness + safety) surfaced as the canonical multi-objective receipt. **[[DPO]]** mechanism: no reward model, no RL loop — compare trainable model against a frozen **reference model**; token-level log-probability shift between them on chosen vs rejected → optimize trainable to be more confident on chosen / less confident on rejected. Forward-looks at [[ORPO]] (Hong, Lee & Thorne 2024, arXiv:2403.07691) as the SFT + DPO collapse into a single training pass. **Generative-LLM evaluation primer**: word-level metrics ([[Perplexity]] / [[ROUGE]] / [[bleu|BLEU]] / [[BERTScore]] — limitations *"do not account for consistency, fluency, creativity, or even correctness"*); public benchmarks (Table 12-1: [[MMLU]] / [[GSM8K]] / [[HellaSwag]] / [[TruthfulQA]] / [[HumanEval]] / [[GLUE]]); leaderboards ([[OpenLLMLeaderboard]]); [[LLMAsAJudge|LLM-as-a-judge]] (Zheng et al. NeurIPS 2024 — MT-Bench / Chatbot Arena); human evaluation via [[ChatbotArena|Chatbot Arena]] (Chiang et al. 2024, arXiv:2403.04132) — crowdsourced pairwise preferences → [[EloRating|Elo]] over 800k+ votes; [[GoodhartsLaw|Goodhart's Law]] (Strathern 1997) as the evaluation-discipline parable; *"you are the best evaluator"* with the Alammar (Arabic) + Grootendorst (Dutch) native-language-eval anecdote.

## [2026-05-23] ingest | Hands-On LLMs Ch09: Multimodal Large Language Models
- **Source**: `raw/books/hands-on-llm/ch09-multimodal-llms.md` — Chapter 9 of *Hands-On Large Language Models* ([[JayAlammar|Jay Alammar]] & [[MaartenGrootendorst|Maarten Grootendorst]], [[OReilly|O'Reilly Media]] 2024, ISBN 978-1-098-15096-9). The wiki's **ninth chapter from *Hands-On LLMs*** (after Chs 1–8) and **the book's vision-language chapter** — the only chapter that extends the wiki's existing text-only LLM coverage to **multimodal models that accept images**. Closes **Part II** of the book before opening **Part III** on training and fine-tuning.
- **Source page**: [[hands-on-llm-ch09-multimodal-llms]].
- **Scope**: Three architecturally distinct moves walked intuition → mechanism → runnable code:
  - **(1) [[VisionTransformer|Vision Transformer (ViT)]]** (Dosovitskiy et al. 2020, arXiv:2010.11929) — the [[transformer|Transformer]] encoder applied to images by tokenizing the image into [[PatchEmbedding|16×16 patches]] and treating patch embeddings the same way as text token embeddings. **The structural punchline**: *"the moment the embeddings are passed to the encoder, they are treated as if they were textual tokens. From that point forward, there is no difference in how a text or image trains"* — the wiki's cleanest statement of why the Transformer machinery generalizes across modalities and the structural precondition for adapter-style multimodal LLMs.
  - **(2) [[CLIP|Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP)]]** (Radford et al. 2021) — the multimodal *embedding* model that projects images and texts into the same 512-dim vector space via [[ContrastiveLearning|contrastive learning]] on (image, caption) pairs. Demonstrated via [[OpenCLIP]] (`openai/clip-vit-base-patch32`) using `CLIPTokenizerFast` / `CLIPProcessor` / `CLIPModel` on an AI-generated puppy-in-the-snow image — L2-normalize-then-dot-product gives **0.33 similarity** (high in CLIP's distribution, even though sounds low — chapter walks a 3×3 similarity matrix to resolve the apparent paradox). Codifies the wiki-novel observation *"in CLIP, the [CLS] token is actually used to represent the image embedding"* (inverse of [[bert|BERT]]'s convention). Names **four CLIP applications**: [[ZeroShotClassification|zero-shot classification]], clustering, search, generation ([[StableDiffusion|Stable Diffusion]] cited as canonical downstream generative use). [[SentenceTransformers|sentence-transformers]]' `SentenceTransformer("clip-ViT-B-32")` named as the few-lines easy-mode wrapper.
  - **(3) [[BLIP2|BLIP-2]]** (Li et al. 2023) — the multimodal *generative* model that bridges a **frozen [[VisionTransformer|ViT]]** and a **frozen LLM** (OPT-2.7b from [[meta]]) via the trainable **[[QFormer|Querying Transformer (Q-Former)]]** + a linear projection. Demonstrated via [[Salesforce|Salesforce]]'s `Salesforce/blip2-opt-2.7b` checkpoint loaded via `transformers.Blip2ForConditionalGeneration` + `AutoProcessor` in `torch.float16`. **Two-stage training**: Stage 1 = Q-Former representation learning on three joint objectives ([[ImageTextContrastive|image-text contrastive]] / [[ImageTextMatching|image-text matching]] / [[ImageGroundedTextGeneration|image-grounded text generation]]); Stage 2 = LLM soft-prompting where the Q-Former's learnable embeddings serve as **[[SoftVisualPrompt|soft visual prompts]]** that condition the LLM. The wiki's first runnable instance of soft-prompting where the soft prompt is **derived from a non-text encoder**.
  - **Generalization to the [[MultimodalLLM|adapter-on-frozen-encoder family]]**: Ch 9 explicitly names [[LLaVA15|LLaVA]] (2-layer MLP projector + Vicuna-13B per Liu et al. 2024) and [[Idefics2|Idefics 2]] (Mistral 7B backbone per Laurençon et al. 2024) as siblings of BLIP-2. The chapter's cleanest formulation of the family: *"Both visual LLMs, although having different architectures, connect pretrained CLIP-like visual encoders with textual LLMs. The goal of these architectures is to project visual features from the input images to language embeddings such that they can be used as the input for an LLM."*
  - **Two BLIP-2 use cases**: **(a) [[ImageCaptioning|Image captioning]]** — supercar image → *"an orange supercar driving on the road at sunset"*; Rorschach inkblot → *"a black and white ink drawing of a bat"*. **(b) [[VisualQuestionAnswering|VQA]] / multimodal chat** — interface trick is to prompt the `Blip2Processor` with both `image` and `text`; second-turn worked example *"What would it cost me to drive that car?"* → *"$1,000,000"* (highly specific). Multi-turn chat implemented by concatenating prior `Question: ... Answer: ...` turns into the prompt; chapter closes with an `ipywidgets`-based fixed-image chatbot demo.
  - **Forward-reference to Ch 10**: *"as we will see in Chapter 10, to make sure the representations are as accurate as possible, negative examples ... should also be included in the training process"* — Ch 10 (training and fine-tuning embedding models) is forward-referenced for the negatives / loss-form treatment.

- **Source**: `raw/books/hands-on-llm/ch08-semantic-search-and-rag.md` — Chapter 8 of *Hands-On Large Language Models* ([[JayAlammar|Jay Alammar]] & [[MaartenGrootendorst|Maarten Grootendorst]], [[OReilly|O'Reilly Media]] 2024, ISBN 978-1-098-15096-9). - **Source page**: [[hands-on-llm-ch08-semantic-search-and-rag]].
- **Scope**: Three architecturally distinct but composable retrieval families walked intuition → runnable code → caveats → evaluation:
  - **(1) [[DenseRetrieval|Dense retrieval]]** — embed query + documents, find nearest neighbors. Worked on a 15-sentence Wikipedia *Interstellar* corpus via [[Cohere]] `co.embed(input_type="search_document" / "search_query")` (4,096-dim vectors) → [[FAISS|`faiss.IndexFlatL2`]]. **Signature demonstration**: query *"how precise was the science"* returns the **correct** *"praise from many astronomers for its scientific accuracy and portrayal of theoretical astrophysics"* via dense retrieval but the **wrong** *"Interstellar is a 2014 epic science fiction film..."* via [[BM25]] (which over-weights the literal word *"science"*). Three caveats: out-of-distribution → [[SimilarityThreshold|similarity threshold]]; exact-phrase weakness → [[HybridSearch|hybrid search]]; domain transfer is hard. [[Chunking]] design space: one-vector-per-document (slice/average) vs multiple-vectors-per-document (sentence/paragraph/overlapping/LLM-driven). [[ApproximateNearestNeighbor|ANN]] libraries ([[Annoy]] / [[FAISS]]) vs [[VectorDatabase|vector databases]] ([[Weaviate]] / [[Pinecone]]) on the **CRUD-and-no-rebuild** axis.
  - **(2) [[ReRanking|Reranking]]** — *"an easier way to incorporate language models is as a final step inside their search pipeline ... it's in fact what Microsoft Bing added to achieve the improvements to search results using BERT-like models."* Worked example via Cohere's `co.rerank` endpoint — no training/tuning required. Headline efficacy: *"on a multilingual benchmark like [[MIRACL]], a reranker can boost performance from 36.5 to 62.8, measured as [[NDCG|nDCG@10]]"* (≈2× lift). Mechanism: [[CrossEncoder|cross-encoder]] (query + result jointly) → relevance score [0,1] = **classification problem** (Ch 4 → Ch 8 continuity). Reference architecture: [[MonoBERT|monoBERT]] (*"Multi-stage document ranking with BERT"*).
  - **(3) [[rag|RAG]]** — structural extension from search by adding an LLM at the end; *"[[GroundedGeneration|grounded generation]] because the retrieved relevant information we provide the LLM establishes a certain context that grounds the LLM in the domain we're interested in."* Managed-RAG via [[Cohere]] `co.chat(message=query, documents=docs_dict)` — produces **automatic span-level [[CitationGeneration|citations]]** (`ChatCitation(start=21, end=36, text='worldwide gross', document_ids=['doc_0'])`) — the wiki's first runnable demonstration. Local-RAG via [[Phi3Mini|Phi-3]] + [[BGESmallEnV15|`BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5`]] + [[FAISS]] + [[LangChain|`langchain.RetrievalQA.from_chain_type(chain_type='stuff', ...)`]] — the wiki's first runnable RetrievalQA receipt.
  - **(4) Retrieval evaluation** — three components required: text archive + queries + [[RelevanceJudgment|relevance judgments]]. [[PrecisionAtK|precision-at-k]] → [[AveragePrecision|average precision]] → [[MAP|mean average precision]] walked step-by-step; [[NDCG]] as graded-relevance alternative.
  - **(5) Advanced RAG continuum** (delegation-increasing): [[QueryRewriting]] (penguins/dolphins essay → *"Where do dolphins live"*) → [[MultiQueryRAG]] (Nvidia 2020 vs 2023 → two parallel queries) → [[MultiHopRAG]] (largest car manufacturers 2023 → Toyota/VW/Hyundai → three EV-followups) → [[QueryRouting]] (HR → Notion, customer → Salesforce) → [[AgenticRAG]] (LLM-as-agent with read+write tool symmetry). **Capability-ceiling caveat**: *"likely only the largest managed models may be able to attempt this behavior"* — same agent-capability-cliff observation as Ch 7's *"Phi-3-mini is not sufficient"* for ReAct.
  - **(6) [[RAGEvaluation|RAG evaluation]]** — four-axis taxonomy per [[NelsonFLiu|Liu]], Zhang & [[PercyLiang|Liang]] 2023 *"Evaluating verifiability in generative search engines"* (arXiv:2304.09848): [[Fluency]] / [[PerceivedUtility|Perceived Utility]] / [[CitationRecall|Citation Recall]] / [[CitationPrecision|Citation Precision]]; automated via [[llmasjudge|LLM-as-a-judge]] with [[RAGAS|Ragas]] adding [[Faithfulness]] + [[AnswerRelevance|Answer Relevance]].
- **Generative-search examples named**: [[Perplexity]], Microsoft Bing AI, Google [[gemini|Gemini]].

- **Scope**: The book's **Transformer-internals deep-dive** — intuition-first walkthrough of the autoregressive decoder-only LLM with a runnable dissection of [[Phi3Mini|Phi-3-mini]]. Five themes:
  - **(1) The three top-level components** — [[Tokenizer|tokenizer]] → stack of [[transformer|Transformer blocks]] → [[LMHead|LM head]] — with `print(model)` revealing 32,064 vocab × 3,072 dim × 32 `Phi3DecoderLayer` blocks containing fused `qkv_proj`, `Phi3RotaryEmbedding`, `Phi3MLP` (SiLU-activated gated MLP), `Phi3RMSNorm` pre-norm placement, and a `Linear(3072 → 32064)` LM head. Worked example: *"The capital of France is"* → `Paris` via `lm_head_output[0, -1].argmax(-1)`.
  - **(2) Parallel [[TokenStream|token-stream]] processing + [[KVCache|KV cache]]** — count of streams = [[ContextLength|context length]]; cross-stream interaction only in attention; only the last stream's output feeds the LM head. KV cache empirical measurement: **4.5 s with `use_cache=True` vs 21.8 s with `use_cache=False`** on Colab T4 / Phi-3-mini / 100 tokens — ~5× speedup.
  - **(3) [[selfattention|Self-attention]] in two pedagogical steps** — relevance scoring (query × keys matrix → softmax) then combining information (weighted sum of value vectors). Three projection matrices ([[QueryProjection|Q]] / [[KeyProjection|K]] / [[ValueProjection|V]]) are the learned attention parameters. [[multiheadattention|Multi-head attention]] runs this in parallel per [[AttentionHead|attention head]]. Decoder attention is causal (vs bidirectional [[bert|BERT]]).
  - **(4) [[FeedForwardNetwork|FFN]] as memorization-and-interpolation engine** ("The Shawshank ___" → `Redemption`; FFN stores facts, attention handles context — "The dog chased the squirrel because it ___").
  - **(5) Modern Transformer block recipe** — [[LocalAttention|local/sparse]] (used by [[GPT3|GPT-3]] every other block) / [[SlidingWindowAttention|sliding-window]] / [[multiqueryattention|MQA]] / [[GroupedQueryAttention|GQA]] (used by [[Llama|Llama 2/3]]); [[FlashAttention|FlashAttention]] + [[FlashAttention2|-2]] GPU kernel; [[PreNorm|pre-norm]] + [[RMSNorm]] + [[SwiGLU]] + [[RoPE|rotary positional embeddings]] (applied at attention step, not at input); [[SequencePacking|sequence packing]] as the training-time pressure motivating relative-aware positional encodings.
- **Key empirical claims**: 5× speedup from KV cache on Phi-3-mini/T4/100 tokens; Phi-3 architecture is 32 layers × 3072 dim × ~2.67× FFN expansion (SwiGLU-style); the modern block recipe (pre-norm + RMSNorm + SwiGLU + GQA + RoPE) is the canonical 2024 default per Llama 2 / 3 deployment.

## [2026-05-22] ingest | Prompt Optimization Is a Coin Flip — Diagnosing When It Helps in Compound AI Systems (Zhang et al., AWS + HSBC, arXiv 2026)
- **Source**: `raw/papers/2604.14585v1.pdf` (copied from `~/Downloads/2604.14585v1.pdf`, 732KB) → [[2604.14585-prompt-optimization-coin-flip]] (arXiv:2604.14585v1, 17 Apr 2026; 9-page main + 3-page appendix).
- **Authors**: [[XingZhang|Zhang]] (first), [[GuanghuiWang|Wang]], [[YanweiCui|Cui]] ([[AWSGenerativeAIInnovationCenter|AWS GenAI Innovation Center]]) + [[WeiQiu|Qiu]], [[ZiyuanLi|Li]], [[BingZhu|Zhu]] ([[HSBC]] Technology Center China) + [[PeiyangHe|He]] (corresponding, AWS, `peiyan@amazon.com`).
- **Scope**: First controlled empirical audit of [[PromptOptimization|prompt optimization]] in [[CompoundAISystem|compound AI systems]]. Tests Assumption A (individual prompts worth optimizing) and Assumption B (prompts interact, requiring joint optimization).
- **Headline statistics**: (a) **49% of 72 optimization runs on [[ClaudeHaiku45|Claude Haiku 4.5]] score below zero-shot** (binomial $p = 0.91$); 14/24 on [[AmazonNovaLite|Amazon Nova Lite]]. (b) $A \times B$ ANOVA interaction **non-significant in all 6 model×task conditions** ($p > 0.52$, all $F < 1.0$, 0.18–2.15% of total variance). (c) Only 1 of 4 tasks ([[HelpSteer2]], JSON rubric, +6.8 [[EvoPrompt]]) beats zero-shot reliably; the [[CanButDoesntPattern|"can but doesn't"]] pattern.
- **Methods**: Study 1 = 3 tasks × $10 \times 10$ prompt grid × $n=30$ samples → two-way ANOVA. Study 2 = 4 tasks × 6 optimizers × 3 repeats; 20 train / 100 test. Executors [[ClaudeHaiku45|Haiku 4.5]] + [[AmazonNovaLite|Nova Lite]]; judge [[ClaudeSonnet46|Claude Sonnet 4.6]].
- **Constructive contribution**: Two-stage [[CompoundAIDiagnostic|practitioner decision framework]] — Stage 1 [[ANOVAVarianceDecomposition|ANOVA coupling test]] (~$80, 1 day) → Stage 2 [[HeadroomTest|headroom test]] (~$5, 10 min). Replaces default joint-optimization assumption.
- **Methodological contribution**: [[ANOVAVarianceDecomposition|ANOVA variance decomposition]] proposed as a falsifiable evaluation protocol for compositional behavior in multi-agent systems.
- **Negative result**: The paper introduces [[PROSEOptimizer|PROSE]] (the authors' own risk-aware evolutionary optimizer with Sharpe + DRO fitness) and shows it offers no measurable advantage over simpler methods — a deliberate test of the *"risk-aware selection helps"* hypothesis.
- **Meta-finding**: [[ModelSpecificityShelfLife|Optimization effects are model-specific]] — which agent matters, which task benefits, which method works all reverse with the executor model. Prompt optimization strategies have shelf life shorter than model release cycle.
- **New concept pages (20)**: [[AgentCoupling]], [[ANOVAVarianceDecomposition]], [[HeadroomTest]], [[CanButDoesntPattern]], [[CoinFlipOptimization]], [[JointOptimization]], [[IndependentOptimization]], [[CompoundAIDiagnostic]], [[ModelSpecificityShelfLife]], [[PROSEOptimizer]], [[TextGrad]], [[GPTSwarm]], [[Helix]], [[PromptBreeder]], [[ProTeGi]], [[XSum]], [[MBPP]], [[HelpSteer2]], [[WildBench]], [[FeedbackBench]].
- **New entity pages (13)**: [[XingZhang]], [[GuanghuiWang]], [[YanweiCui]], [[WeiQiu]], [[ZiyuanLi]], [[BingZhu]], [[PeiyangHe]], [[AWSGenerativeAIInnovationCenter]], [[HSBC]], [[ClaudeHaiku45]], [[AmazonNovaLite]], [[ClaudeSonnet46]], [[Nie2026Iterative]].
- **Updated in place**: [[CompoundAISystem]] (adds empirical independence result + [[ANOVAVarianceDecomposition]] protocol), [[PromptOptimization]] (adds 49% coin-flip empirical baseline + diagnostic gating + 5 new sibling optimizers), [[MIPROv2]] (adds 2026 empirical caveat about cross-module joint optimization being untested), [[GEPA]] (adds empirical context about [[CanButDoesntPattern|exploitable output structure]] dependence), [[BetterTogether]] (adds 2026 cross-axis coupling caveat), [[hotpotqa]] (adds Study 1 ANOVA decomposition showing smallest interaction despite *a priori* tight-coupling prediction), [[Amazon]] (adds [[AWSGenerativeAIInnovationCenter]] + [[AmazonNovaLite]]), [[anthropic]] (adds [[ClaudeHaiku45]] + [[ClaudeSonnet46]] as third-party study targets).

- **Overview**: new banner at top — describes both studies, the coin-flip statistic, the [[CanButDoesntPattern|"can but doesn't" pattern]], the two-stage [[CompoundAIDiagnostic|diagnostic framework]], and the contrast with prior MIPRO / BetterTogether / GEPA / Neural-ArchEHR-QA optimization successes.
- **Contradictions flagged**: (1) vs [[2406.11695-mipro|MIPRO]] Lesson 2 ("joint optimization wins overall") — partially resolved by setting: MIPRO's within-module instruction × demo joint is not directly challenged, but across-module joint optimization premise is. (2) vs [[2407.10930-better-together|BetterTogether]]'s bi-axial alternation — Zhang et al. don't test the $\Pi \times \Theta$ axis directly but the same coupling assumption is at stake. (3) vs [[2507.19457-gepa|GEPA]]'s headline gains — open question whether GEPA's reflective mutation crosses the 2-pt headroom threshold on free-form tasks. (4) vs the joint-optimization premise behind [[TextGrad]] / [[DSPy]] / [[GPTSwarm]] / [[Helix]] — directly tested and falsified for two-agent feed-forward pipelines. (5) The "PROSE risk-aware design improves robustness" hypothesis — empirically rejected by the paper's own data.
- **Scope limits flagged**: two-agent feed-forward only; mid-tier models ([[ClaudeHaiku45|Haiku 4.5]] + [[AmazonNovaLite|Nova Lite]]); $K=10$ whole-prompt substitutions; 20 training questions; natural-language inter-agent communication.

Sibling structural-falsification paper to [[2604.27707-agentic-memory-is-a-memo]] and [[2605.10698-bystander-effect-mas]] — all three audit a prevailing compound-AI claim with a falsifiable structural test and find the claim mostly fails.

## [2026-05-22] ingest | DSPy Tutorial — Managing Conversation History
- **Source**: `https://dspy.ai/tutorials/conversation_history/` → `raw/dspy-conversation-history.md` → [[dspy-conversation-history|wiki/sources/dspy-conversation-history.md]].
- **Scope**: First wiki-corpus [[DSPy]] page anchored to a *tutorial* rather than a *Learn* reference or paper. Scopes [[DSPy]] at the **multi-turn chatbot** application layer.
- **Load-bearing disclosure**: *"DSPy does not provide such functionality out of the box, meaning users are required to manage the conversation history on their own."* [[DSPyModules|`dspy.Module`]] has **no** built-in inter-turn state capture — the developer owns the [[DSPyHistory|`dspy.History`]] instance lifecycle.
- **Primitive**: [[DSPyHistory|`dspy.History`]] — a [[DSPySignatures|Signature]] field type with a single attribute `messages: list[dict[str, Any]]`. DSPy-special type tier-five alongside [[DSPyImage|`dspy.Image`]].
- **Two essential procedures**: (i) declare `history: dspy.History = dspy.InputField()` on the [[DSPySignatures|Signature]]; (ii) instantiate `dspy.History(messages=[])` at session start, append `history.messages.append({"question": question, **outputs})` after each turn, re-pass on every call.
- **Few-shot rendering disclosure**: history-bearing [[DSPyExample|`dspy.Example`]] demos render as a **single turn with the messages serialized as JSON** rather than expanded into multiple `role=user`/`role=assistant` turns — *"DSPy renders the history as a single message in the few-shot examples to maintain compatibility with the OpenAI standard format."* Keeps prompt envelopes bounded under [[BootstrapFewShot]] / [[BootstrapFewShotWithRandomSearch]] / [[MIPROv2]] demo budgets; preserves the OpenAI `messages=[...]` shape the [[LiteLLM]] layer expects.
- **Position in DSPy application stack**: fills the missing **single-agent multi-turn** rung (rung 3 of 6) between [[DSPyPredict|single-call]] (rungs 1–2) and [[CoSTORM|multi-agent collaborative discourse]] (rung 5).

This is **structurally novel** relative to conventional ML hyperparameter optimization, where a `sklearn.GridSearchCV` doesn't typically consume another `GridSearchCV`'s output as input. DSPy can scale **both** *pre-inference-time compute* (the optimizer's budget) and *inference-time compute* (the ensemble's vote) from a single optimizer run — the `Ensemble` + top-k-extraction pattern operationalizes this directly. `BetterTogether` is what happens when this composability is **formalized as a sequence schedule** (prompt → weight → prompt).

- Source: `sources/dis-4-4-2-subtraction.md` ([[DiveIntoSystems]] Ch 4.4.2 — **second subsection** of [[dis-4-4-arithmetic|Ch 4.4 *Binary Integer Arithmetic*]] inside **Ch 4 *Binary and Data Representation***).
- URL: https://diveintosystems.org/book/C4-Binary/arithmetic_subtraction.html
- Authors: [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]].
- New concept pages: **1** — [[BinarySubtraction]] (the base-2 subtraction operation implemented as **addition of the [[TwosComplement|two's-complement]] negation** $A + (-B)$; reuses the [[dis-4-4-1-addition|Ch 4.4.1]] [[BinaryAddition|adder]] via a row of [[XOR|XOR]] gates on operand B (the *flip-all-bits* step) plus [[CarryIn|`CarryIn`]] = 1 on the LSB adder (the *add one* step), folding the [[TwosComplement|two's-complement]] negation into the addition at **zero extra arithmetic hardware**; mode-switching unifies to one wire `Subtract`; worked examples $7 - 3 = 4$ and $7 - (-3) = 10$ verify all four sign combinations work via the same circuit — the [[dis-4-4-arithmetic|Ch 4.4]] interpretation-invariance reapplied; MSB carry-out *"doesn't necessarily indicate overflow"* in subtraction mode — full [[IntegerOverflow|overflow]] rule deferred).
- Updated: [[DiveIntoSystems]] (corpus 39 → **40 chapters**; Connections section added Ch 4.4.2 bullet above Ch 4.4.1; corpus-status paragraph extended). Skipped overview per task scope.

- Key payoffs: (1) cashes in [[dis-4-4-1-addition|Ch 4.4.1]]'s `CarryIn` hook — `CarryIn` was hard-wired to `0` for ordinary addition but exists architecturally *because of* subtraction; this chapter delivers on that promise. (2) the **add/subtract unit** mode-switches on a single `Subtract` wire: `Subtract = 0` → ordinary addition ($A + B$); `Subtract = 1` → XOR-row flips B and LSB `CarryIn = 1` → $A + (\overline{B} + 1) = A - B$. (3) **sign-combination universality** — the same circuit handles $A - B$ for all four sign combinations (`+ − +`, `+ − −`, `− − +`, `− − −`) without special-case logic, reapplying [[dis-4-4-arithmetic|Ch 4.4]] interpretation-invariance to the subtraction case. (4) **MSB carry-out semantics shift** between addition and subtraction modes — anticipates the [[IntegerOverflow|overflow]] story (worked example $7 - (-3) = \mathtt{0b1010}$ has MSB=1 but is the correct unsigned $10$).

## [2026-05-17] ingest | ParProcBook Appendix B: Review of Matrix Algebra

- Source page created: `wiki/sources/parproc-appB-matrix-algebra.md` — Appendix B (pp. 313–320) of *Programming on Parallel Machines* by [[NormMatloff]]. Eight-section math primer: §B.1 notation + [[MatrixMultiplication|matrix multiplication]] (inner product definition, non-commutativity); §B.2 [[MatrixTranspose|transpose]] ($(AB)' = B'A'$, orthogonal matrices $U^{-1}=U'$); §B.3 [[LinearIndependence|linear independence]]; §B.4 [[Determinant|determinants]] (recursive cofactor expansion, base case $sv-tu$); §B.5 [[MatrixInversion|matrix inverse]] (identity matrix, invertibility conditions, $(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$, QR decomposition route); §B.6 [[Eigenvalue|eigenvalues]] and [[Eigenvector|eigenvectors]] ($AX=\lambda X$, diagonalizability conditions for symmetric and distinct-eigenvalue cases); §B.7 [[Rank|rank]] ($\text{rk}(A')=\text{rk}(A)$, $\text{rk}(A)\leq\min(r,s)$, $\text{rk}(A'A)=\text{rk}(A)$); §B.8 R syntax (`%*%`, `t()`, `solve()`, `eigen()`, `qr()`, `qr.solve()`, `diag()`).
- 2 new concept pages: [[MatrixTranspose]], [[LinearIndependence]].
- Extended existing pages: [[Determinant]] (§B.4 recursive formula section + connections), [[Rank]] (expanded from stub — §B.7 formal properties + R syntax + connections), [[Eigenvalue]] (§B.6 diagonalizability conditions + R syntax + footnote on SVD), [[Eigenvector]] (§B.6 orthogonality for symmetric case), [[MatrixInversion]] (§B.5 definitions + QR route + R syntax + connections).
- Updated: `wiki/index.md` (source row for parproc-appB, 2 new concept rows, count 299→300), `wiki/log.md` (this entry).
- Contradictions: None. The Ch11 footnote calling singular values "synonyms" for eigenvalues is refined (not contradicted) by the Appendix B footnote directing nonsquare cases to SVD.

## [2026-05-17] ingest | ParProcBook Ch11: Introduction to Parallel Matrix Operations

- Source page created: `wiki/sources/parproc-ch11-parallel-matrix-operations.md` — Ch11 (pp. 235–256) of *Programming on Parallel Machines* by [[NormMatloff]]. Covers partitioned matrices, [[FoxAlgorithm|Fox's algorithm]] (MPI), [[MatrixMultiplication|matrix multiplication]] in [[OpenMP]] / [[CUDA]] (Edgar 500× tiling) / R [[Snow]] / gputools, matrix powers for [[GraphConnectedness|graph connectivity]] / [[FibonacciNumbers|Fibonacci]] / [[MatrixInversion|inversion]], [[GaussianElimination|Gaussian elimination]] and [[JacobiAlgorithm|Jacobi iteration]] for linear systems, [[PowerMethod|power method]] and CULA SVD for [[Eigenvalue|eigenvalues]], [[SparseMatrix|CSR sparse format]], and library survey (CUBLAS, CUSP, CULA, ScalaPACK, OpenBLAS).
- 12 new concept pages: [[PartitionedMatrix]], [[FoxAlgorithm]], [[MatrixMultiplication]], [[GaussianElimination]], [[JacobiAlgorithm]], [[GraphConnectedness]], [[FibonacciNumbers]], [[MatrixInversion]], [[PowerMethod]], [[Eigenvalue]], [[Eigenvector]], [[SparseMatrix]].
- Updated: [[MatrixVectorMultiply]] (sources frontmatter — added parproc-ch11), `wiki/index.md` (Ch11 source row + 12 new concept rows), `wiki/log.md` (this entry).
- Stub superseded: `wiki/concepts/solvinglinearsystemsusinggaussianelimination.md` is now superseded by the full [[GaussianElimination]] page; the stub file is retained for wikilink compatibility.
- Contradictions: (1) Matloff's footnote equating "singular value" to "eigenvalue" is an oversimplification — singular values equal eigenvalues only for symmetric positive semidefinite matrices; noted in [[Eigenvalue]] page. (2) Jacobi convergence condition stated as diagonal dominance is sufficient but not necessary; noted in [[JacobiAlgorithm]] page. No contradictions with prior wiki content.

- Source page created: `wiki/sources/dis-2-8-io.md` — Ch 2.8 of [[DiveIntoSystems]] from https://diveintosystems.org/book/C2-C_depth/IO.html. **Returns to [[CLanguage|C]] I/O** with the depth [[dis-1-2-input-output|Ch 1.2]] deferred — three movements: (1) standard-I/O deepening (expanded [[FormatSpecifier|specifier table]] + [[StandardError|`stderr`]] + [[StreamRedirection|shell redirection]]), (2) full **file-I/O** API on [[FilePointer|`FILE *`]] ([[Fopen|`fopen`]] → [[Fclose|`fclose`]] four-step protocol, [[FileMode|`"r"`/`"w"`/`"a"` modes]], the four function families, [[Fseek|`fseek`]]/[[Rewind|`rewind`]] positioning), (3) the [[ScanfCharClass|`%[...]` / `%Ns` specifier extensions]] — the **robustness fix** for the [[Scanf|`scanf`]] fragility [[dis-1-2-input-output|Ch 1.2]] deferred. Two non-obvious guarantees the chapter pins down: handlers are **software-uncallable** (calling `SysTick();` is a compile error) and `static mut` inside the body is therefore **safe** (the attribute rewrites it to `&mut`; soundness rests on the hardware-only invocation contract precluding reentrancy on a single core — multicore breaks this and needs explicit synchronization). Three worked examples: (1) [[SysTick]] handler counting ticks in a `COUNT` `static mut`, printing over [[ARMSemihosting|semihosting]] on [[QEMU]] via `qemu-system-arm -cpu cortex-m3 -machine lm3s6965evb`, self-terminating after 9 ticks via `debug::exit`; (2) `DefaultHandler(irqn: i16)` override pattern with the architectural-vs-device discriminant (`irqn < 0` ⇒ Cortex-M architectural exception, `irqn ≥ 0` ⇒ device-specific [[Interrupt|IRQ]]); (3) [[HardFault]] post-mortem with the mandatory `fn(&ExceptionFrame) -> !` signature, dumping the [[ExceptionFrame]] (r0…r12, lr, pc, xpsr) over semihosting and cross-referencing `pc = 0x0800094a` against `cargo objdump` to identify the faulting `ldr r0, [r0]` instruction reading `0x3fff_fffe`.

- Content: three named patterns. **`C-ZST-PIN`** — *"GPIO Interfaces … should provide dedicated zero-sized types for each pin on every interface or port, resulting in a zero-cost GPIO abstraction when all pin assignments are statically known"*; each port implements a `split()` method returning a struct whose fields are one [[ZeroSizedType|ZST]] per physical pin — operationalizes [[ZeroSizedType]] / [[ZeroCostAbstraction]] from [[rust-embedded-book-static-guarantees-zero-cost-abstractions]] for [[GPIO]] pins. **`C-ERASED-PIN`** — two-stage type erasure: `PA0::erase_pin(self) -> PA { pin: u8 }` collapses 16 distinct ZSTs into a 1-byte handle (pin identity → runtime); `PA::erase_port(self) -> Pin { port: Port, pin: u8 }` collapses 4 ports into a ≤2-byte handle (port identity → runtime); trades compile-time-pin-distinctness for heterogeneous-collection-ability — `[Pin; N]` / `Vec<Pin>` / `&dyn` trait objects. **`C-PIN-STATE`** — two-axis [[TypeStateProgramming|typestate]] (`Input<Floating|PullUp|PullDown>` and `Output<PushPull|OpenDrain>` via `PhantomData<S>`), with **`into_input` / `into_output`** consuming-`self` transitions **plus** **`with_input_state` / `with_output_state`** scoped-reconfiguration variants (`&mut self` + `FnOnce(&mut PA1<N>) -> R`) for *"temporarily reconfigur[ing] a pin in a different state without moving it"* — the addition over a vanilla builder-style typestate; all bounded by **sealed traits** so users cannot add their own pin states. The three patterns **stack**: a fully-static `PA1<Output<PushPull>>` is a zero-sized handle that survives both erasure stages without losing the typestate parameter — *"both erased and non-erased pin types should provide the same API."*

## [2026-05-16] ingest | The Embedded Rust Book — A little C with your Rust
- Source: `raw/book/src/interoperability/c-with-rust.md` → `wiki/sources/rust-embedded-book-interoperability-c-with-rust.md` (file 39/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — **first leaf** of the *Interoperability* chapter ([[rust-embedded-book-interoperability-index]]); operationalizes calling **C/C++ from Rust** as two orthogonal halves — the Rust-side interface and the host-side C build).
- Content: **(1) Define the interface.** For every C `typedef struct CoolStruct { int x; int y; }` + `void cool_function(int i, char c, CoolStruct* cs);`, emit `#[repr(C)] pub struct CoolStruct { pub x: cty::c_int, pub y: cty::c_int }` ([[ReprC]]) plus an `extern "C" { pub fn cool_function(i: cty::c_int, c: cty::c_char, cs: *mut CoolStruct); }` block ([[ExternC]]). [[RawPointer|Raw pointers]] (`*mut T` / `*const T`) stand in for Rust references (which C cannot represent); `cty::c_int` / `cty::c_char` aliases stand in for platform-variable C primitives (the [[NoStd|`no_std`]]-compatible equivalent of the `core::ffi` aliases [[rust-embedded-book-interoperability-index]] introduced). Auto-generate the whole interface from C headers via [[Bindgen|`bindgen`]] with `--ctypes-prefix=cty` + `--use-core` flags for `#![no_std]` compatibility. **(2) Build the C/C++ to a static archive.** Three branches: already-prebuilt `lib*.a` (just link); complex `make`/`CMake` project (shell out via `std::process::Command` from [[BuildRs|`build.rs`]] and copy the archive into `target/`); small C source set (compile directly via the [[CcCrate|`cc` crate]] — `fn main() { cc::Build::new().file("src/foo.c").compile("foo"); }`). Two design rules: **C++ has no stable ABI for [[Rustc|rustc]]** → use the `C` ABI as the lingua franca even when wrapping C++ (typically via a thin C wrapper layer); **the package may target `thumbv7m-none-eabi` / [[NoStd|`no_std`]] but `build.rs` itself runs on the *host*** — *"This means you may use any Rust crates which will run on your compilation host."* Static archive (`cool-library.a`) is the embedded delivery format because [[BareMetalProgramming|bare-metal]] firmware has no dynamic loader.

## [2026-05-16] ingest | The Embedded Rust Book — A little Rust with your C
- Source: `raw/book/src/interoperability/rust-with-c.md` → `wiki/sources/rust-embedded-book-interoperability-rust-with-c.md` (file 40/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — **second leaf** of the *Interoperability* chapter ([[rust-embedded-book-interoperability-index]]) and the **deliberate mirror** of file 39 ([[rust-embedded-book-interoperability-c-with-rust]]); operationalizes exposing **Rust to C/C++** — the inverse direction of the prior chapter).
- Content: **(1) Build a C-friendly Rust API.** Cargo's `[lib] crate-type = ["cdylib"]` (dynamic — emits `lib<name>.so` / `<name>.dll` / `lib<name>.dylib`) or `["staticlib"]` (static archive — emits `lib<name>.a` / `<name>.lib`) declaration in `Cargo.toml` ([[CrateType]]) selects the output systems-library format; only the first two are C-consumable, and `staticlib` is the only viable form for [[BareMetalProgramming|bare-metal]] firmware. Every exported function carries the canonical attribute triple — `pub` (visibility) + [[NoMangle|`#[no_mangle]`]] (linker — defeats Rust's symbol mangling so the C linker sees the literal source identifier `rust_function` instead of the namespace-and-hash-encoded long form) + [[ExternC|`extern "C"`]] (compiler — switches the function from Rust's unstable internal ABI to the platform C ABI). The canonical shape: `#[no_mangle] pub extern "C" fn rust_function() {}`. This is the **exported** form of `extern "C"` (form 2 of [[ExternC]]) — file 39 covered only the **imported** declaration-block form (form 1). **(2) Embed the produced library in an external build system.** *"This very much depends on your project and/or build system."* Cargo emits the `.so`/`.dll`/`.a` artifact; the host project's `make` / `CMake` / IDE links it like any other system library. The C side needs a matching header — hand-written (`void rust_function();`) or auto-generated by [[Cbindgen|`cbindgen`]] (`github.com/eqrion/cbindgen`), the **inverse-direction** symmetric counterpart to file 39's [[Bindgen|`bindgen`]] (`bindgen`: C → Rust; `cbindgen`: Rust → C). Same C-ABI-as-lingua-franca rule as file 39: *"Because C++ has no stable ABI for the Rust compiler to target, we use `C` for any interoperability between different languages."* Data-marshaling discipline (`#[repr(C)]` on shared structs, `*mut T` / `*const T` raw pointers in place of references, `cty::c_int` aliases for platform-variable C primitives) carries over wholesale from [[rust-embedded-book-interoperability-c-with-rust]].

## [2026-05-16] ingest | The Embedded Rust Book — Optimizations
- Source: `raw/book/src/unsorted/speed-vs-size.md` → `wiki/sources/rust-embedded-book-unsorted-speed-vs-size.md` (file 42/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — **first substantive leaf** of the *Unsorted topics* chapter, immediately after the trivial placeholder opener at file 41 ([[rust-embedded-book-unsorted-index]])).
- Content: Tactical [[Cargo]] / [[Rustc|`rustc`]] reference on the **five [[OptLevel|`opt-level`]] values** (`0` / `1` / `2` / `3` / `"s"` / `"z"`, inherited from clang/LLVM) across **three regimes** — *No optimizations* (`opt-level = 0`, the `dev` profile default — statement-by-statement debugging, `print` works in [[GDB]], but the binary may not fit in [[FlashMemory|Flash]]); *Optimize for speed* (`1` / `2` / `3`, the `release` profile default at `3` — `2` and `3` **unconditionally unroll loops** with no opt-out, `3` adds vectorization + more inlining; loop unrolling costs *"from 26 bytes to 194 for a zero this array loop"* but can *"halve the execution time"*); *Optimize for size* (`"s"` / `"z"` — `"z"` is the smaller of the two, *"these names were inherited from clang / LLVM and are not too descriptive"*). The chapter's **signature trick** is the **`profile-overrides`** Cargo feature that decouples top-crate optimization from dependencies — `[profile.dev.package."*"] opt-level = "z"` keeps the application at `opt-level = 0` debugger-friendly while shrinking all deps (worked example: `.text` 9060 → 3490 bytes, `.rodata` 1708 → 1100 bytes — **6 KiB Flash saved** with no loss of top-crate debuggability); granular form `[profile.dev.package.cortex-m-rt] opt-level = 0` opts a single dep back out for when stepping into it is needed. Two cross-cutting recommendations: **`[profile.release] debug = true`** because *"for bare metal development, debuginfo is zero cost in the sense that it won't occupy space in Flash / ROM"* — symbols stay host-side in the ELF, never reaching the device — so release builds get to keep their breakpoints. **`"s"` / `"z"` slash LLVM's inline threshold** (75 / 25 vs `2`'s 225 and `3`'s 275, as of `rustc` 1.29.0) — hostile to Rust's many small [[ZeroCostAbstraction|zero-cost-abstraction]] functions (`deref`, `as_ref`, newtype wrappers). Workaround: `rustflags = ["-C", "inline-threshold=225"]` in `.cargo/config.toml`. Caveat on `profile-overrides`: *"generic code can sometimes be optimized alongside the crate where it is instantiated, rather than the crate where it is defined"* — monomorphized code is emitted in the *instantiating* crate, so the override may have no effect on heavy generic structs the top crate uses. Composes with `codegen-units = 1` for *"better optimizations"* on dependencies.
- New pages: **1** — 1 concept ([[OptLevel]] — the `rustc -C opt-level=<N>` dial; full regime table, embedded Flash-budget tension story tying together [[FlashMemory]] / [[ZeroCostAbstraction]] / LLVM inline-threshold, the `profile-overrides` recipe with worked example, the `[profile.release] debug = true` bare-metal recommendation, and the generic-instantiation caveat). No new entities.

## [2026-05-16] ingest | The Embedded Rust Book — Performing Math Functionality
- Source: `raw/book/src/unsorted/math.md` → `wiki/sources/rust-embedded-book-unsorted-math.md` (file 43/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — **second substantive leaf** of the *Unsorted topics* chapter, immediately after [[rust-embedded-book-unsorted-speed-vs-size]] at file 42).
- Content: Short single-recipe chapter. With [[RustStandardLibrary|`std`]] available, math methods (`f32::floor` / `f32::sqrt` / `f32::sin` / `f32::exp`) come for free as **inherent methods** on the primitive float types; under [[NoStd|`#![no_std]`]] these methods are unavailable — [[RustCoreLibrary|`core`]] exposes `f32` / `f64` but **not** their transcendental / rounding operations (the canonical reference implementations live in C's `libm` which `core` cannot depend on). The chapter's drop-in fix is the **[[LibmCrate|`libm`]] crate** — a pure-Rust port of C's `libm` re-exposing the same operations as **free functions** (`use libm::{exp, floorf, sin, sqrtf};` then `sqrtf(x)` replaces `x.sqrt()`) callable from any `no_std` crate without a [[GlobalAllocator|global allocator]] or [[RustRuntime|runtime]]. Worked example rewrites the same four-operation `hello`-style program **twice** — once for hosted [[RustStandardLibrary|`std`]] with `println!`, once for [[ARMCortexM|Cortex-M]] `no_std` ([[CortexMRTCrate|`cortex-m-rt`]] + [[CortexMSemihostingCrate|`cortex-m-semihosting`]] + [[PanicHaltCrate|`panic-halt`]] + [[ARMSemihosting|`hprintln!`]]) — the only syntactic delta is **method-call vs free-function** plus the host-I/O macro swap. **Precision suffix follows C convention**: `f`-suffixed = `f32` (`sqrtf`, `floorf`), no-suffix = `f64` (`sin`, `exp`); the example calls `.into()` on `f32` arguments to widen them. Closes with a **five-crate further-reading list** for when scalar `libm` is not enough — [`cmsis-dsp-sys`](https://github.com/jacobrosenthal/cmsis-dsp-sys) (CMSIS DSP bindings, SIMD-accelerated on [[ARMCortexM|Cortex-M4F]]+), [`constgebra`](https://crates.io/crates/constgebra) (`const fn` linalg), [`micromath`](https://github.com/tarcieri/micromath) (compact `no_std` math), [`microfft`](https://crates.io/crates/microfft) (in-place FFT), [`nalgebra`](https://github.com/dimforge/nalgebra) (general-purpose Rust linalg, optional `no_std`). The five-crate list is mentioned in passing, not given individual pages — `libm` is the scalar-transcendental floor of the stack, the rest layer on top. Re-asserts the standing **"don't `debug::exit()` on hardware"** warning from [[rust-embedded-book-start-semihosting]].
- New pages: **1** — 1 entity ([[LibmCrate]] — `rust-lang/libm`, pure-Rust port of C's `libm`; precision-suffix convention table; `core`/`std`/`libm` gap-filler framing; further-reading mention of the five layered-math crates). No new concepts (no [[FloatingPointUnit]] page — the chapter does not actually discuss FPU; `f32` vs `f64` shows up only implicitly in `libm`'s `f`-suffix API split).

## [2026-05-17] ingest | ParProcBook Ch2: Recurring Performance Issues

- Source: pp. 31–42 of *Programming on Parallel Machines* by [[NormMatloff]] ([[UCDavis]]); short twelve-page chapter installing the vocabulary the rest of the book uses to talk about *why parallel code is slow*.
- New source page: [[parproc-ch02-recurring-performance-issues]].
- New concept pages (10): [[LoadBalancing]], [[CommunicationBottleneck]], [[EmbarrassinglyParallel]], [[WorkStealing]], [[Latency]], [[Bandwidth]], [[StaticTaskAssignment]], [[DynamicTaskAssignment]], [[IterativeAlgorithms]], [[MatrixVectorMultiply]].
- Key takeaways: (1) communication is *always* a potential bottleneck — bus / [[CoherentCaches|cache-coherency]] on shared-memory, network latency on clusters, CPU↔GPU + on-device contention on [[GPU|GPUs]]; (2) the headline thesis — **[[StaticTaskAssignment|static (but possibly randomized) task assignment]] typically beats [[DynamicTaskAssignment|dynamic]]** — justified by the $O(1/\sqrt{m})$ chunk-time concentration argument and an 8000×8000 Mandelbrot timing table (`static` 47.8s, `dynamic` 21.4s, `guided` 29.6s, `random` 15.7s); (3) the meaning of [[EmbarrassinglyParallel|"embarrassingly parallel"]] has *drifted* from "trivially decomposable" to "low [[CommunicationBottleneck|communication]] needs" — the Ch1 prime-finder qualifies as the former but *not* the latter; (4) [[Latency]] and [[Bandwidth]] are two independent dimensions of communication delay, with [[NormMatloff|Matloff]]'s bridge analogy (cars-per-time vs cars-cross-time); (5) the historical [[SharedMemoryArchitecture|shared-memory]]-vs-[[MessagePassingArchitecture|message-passing]] scalability claim is now scrambled by [[GPU]]s demonstrating *"extremely good scalability with shared-memory."*
- Index: bumped Sources 289→290 and Concepts 1056→1066; new entries inserted alphabetically under Sources (after [[parproc-ch01-intro-parallel-processing]]) and under Concepts.
- Overview: NOT updated per task scope; this chapter expands an existing thread ([[parproc-ch01-intro-parallel-processing]]) rather than opening a new synthesis axis.
- Contradictions: §2.6 explicitly retracts the historical *"message-passing is more scalable"* community consensus, citing [[GPU]]s — worth flagging for downstream chapters. §2.3.1 explicitly disqualifies the prime-finder from [[parproc-ch01-intro-parallel-processing]] §1.5.1 as embarrassingly-parallel under the new meaning. The "dynamic-is-better-because-flexible" cultural intuition (implicit in [[Cilk]]-adjacent work-stealing literature) is contradicted by the chapter's math + Mandelbrot timing table.
- Post-validation: all 10 new concept pages exist on disk; the source page's [[wikilinks]] resolve to either the new pages or to pre-existing pages ([[NormMatloff]], [[UCDavis]], [[parproc-ch01-intro-parallel-processing]], [[OpenMP]], [[GPU]], [[MPI]], [[Snow]], [[SharedMemoryArchitecture]], [[MessagePassingArchitecture]], [[CoherentCaches]], [[Barrier]], [[CriticalSection]], [[ScatterGather]]); 4 wikilinks point to pages that do not yet exist as files but are referenced from prior wiki content ([[Cilk]], [[Mandelbrot]], [[MemoryAllocation]], [[LatencyHiding]]) — these are valid lazy stubs, intentionally out of scope for this Ch2 ingest.

- Key takeaways: (1) the chapter is a forward-reference resolver — [[CoherentCaches]] / [[NUMA]] / [[Barrier]] from Ch1 and the "memory banks" / "cache-coherency" items deferred by Ch2 §2.8 all get their substantive treatment here; (2) the interconnect scaling table (bus $O(1)/O(1)/O(1)$ vs omega $O(\log n)/O(n)/O(n\log n)$ vs crossbar $O(n)/O(n)/O(n^2)$) is the most reused diagram of the chapter; (3) Matloff carefully separates **[[CacheCoherency|coherency]]** (multi-cache, one address — "do caches agree?") from **[[MemoryConsistency|consistency]]** (one variable — "when does a write become visible?") — they are distinct timing-level problems; (4) [[MESI]] is given in full transition-table detail, including the notable rule that a *write miss does NOT bring the block in*; (5) [[FalseSharing]] is the cache-line-granularity pathology that motivates [[ProcessorAffinity]] and [[JIAJIA]]'s multi-writer feature; (6) the [[JIAJIA]] case study is unusually detailed for a textbook — page-based + scope-consistent + home-based + multi-writer, with the diff/twin reconciliation mechanism and Treadmarks-measured 167 μs twin / 686 μs diff costs; (7) the chapter's three barrier iterations operationalize a recurring [[NormMatloff|Matloff]] pedagogy — *show the obvious bug, then the subtler one, then the correct fix*.
- Index: bumped Sources 290→291; added 15 new Concept entries inserted alphabetically.
- Overview: NOT updated per task scope; this chapter resolves forward-references from Ch1/Ch2 rather than opening a new synthesis axis.
- Contradictions: no contradictions with prior wiki content (this chapter delivers what Ch1/Ch2 promised). One internal-to-the-book tension flagged: §3.8's *"multicore is just SMP"* claim is best read as a software-API statement, not a microarchitectural one — §3.10 ([[ProcessorAffinity]]) and §3.5.3 ([[FalseSharing]]) are tools that matter *more* on multicore than on discrete-CPU SMPs. One historical-accuracy aside: §3.6 claims *"recent Pentium models use Sequential Consistency"* — x86-TSO (a relaxation permitting store-buffer reordering of younger loads past older stores to different addresses) is the documented Intel model since at least the mid-2000s. Not a wiki-internal contradiction.

- Key Ch5 architectural claims: GPUs *run hundreds or thousands of threads at once* vs Ch4's quad-core 4 threads; SM/SP hierarchy = *multi-multiprocessor machine*; warps are 32 threads in SIMT lockstep with [[ThreadDivergence|divergence]] as the within-warp *performance killer*; SM is *an OS in hardware* doing latency hiding by warp-swap on memory stall, with nearly-free context switches because each warp has its own register set → granularity flip: **CUDA wants many small threads, OpenMP wants few large threads**; shared memory is a *programmer-managed cache*; inter-block sync is hard (only atomic ops or host-roundtrip); 128–256 threads/block rule of thumb, must be multiple of 32.

- Key takeaways: (1) **the array-decay mechanism is the unifying primitive** — `T arr[N]` becomes `T *` at the call boundary, which is what makes pass-by-reference (Ch 1.5) = pass-by-value of a pointer (Ch 2.2) and what makes static and dynamic 1D arrays share a parameter signature (Ch 2.4); Ch 2.5 names it explicitly with the *"C copies the value of the base address to the parameter"* quote; (2) **row-major layout drives the parameter rule** — `&m[i][j] = m_base + i*M + j` needs `M`, hence trailing dimensions are mandatory in 2D parameter declarations; (3) **the two dynamic 2D forms have non-interchangeable parameter types** — single-`malloc` `int *` is *not* `int **`, and a static `int m[N][M]` decays to `int (*)[M]` which is *also* neither — three distinct types with three distinct parameter signatures, despite all three supporting some form of `arr[i][j]` (the single-malloc form being the exception that requires `arr[i*M+j]`); (4) **the syntactic-vs-memory tradeoff** is the Ch 2.5 headline design lesson — `arr[i][j]` ergonomics cost N+1 heap headers + worse cache locality + non-contiguous rows; (5) **ragged 2D requires the array-of-arrays form** — rows of different lengths are inexpressible with a single contiguous malloc; (6) **the lost-bound property of decayed pointers** is the root cause of the corpus's load-bearing security thread (Ch 1.5 [[Strcpy]] / Ch 2.6 [[BufferOverflow]]) — surfaced cleanly on the new [[ArrayDecay]] page.

- Key takeaways: (1) **MPI is an API standard, not an implementation** — MPICH (active, network/platform tailoring), LAM (discontinued → Open MPI), Open MPI (active, *"not to be confused with [[OpenMP]]"*), MVAPICH ([[Infiniband]]-tuned), Intel MPI; (2) **[[SPMD]] is the canonical execution model** — every node runs the same compiled binary, branching by rank; (3) **collectives subsume hand-coded send/recv loops** — the §8.6.1 *Refined Dijkstra* deletes three functions and replaces them with three collective calls; (4) **the 12-op reduce table** — `MPI_MAX` / `MPI_MIN` / `MPI_SUM` / `MPI_PROD` / `MPI_LAND` / `MPI_LOR` / `MPI_LXOR` / `MPI_BAND` / `MPI_BOR` / `MPI_BXOR` / `MPI_MAXLOC` / `MPI_MINLOC`, the `*LOC` variants on `MPI_2INT` pair type; (5) **the exact MPI-standard send semantic is buffer-reusability** — *"`MPI_Send(x,...)` will return only when it is safe for the application program to write over the array which it is using to store its message, i.e. x"* — explicitly NOT *"receiver has the data"*; (6) **synchronous communication can deadlock on tag mismatch**, *"asynchronous communication is considered unsafe in MPI terminology"* but most code accepts the buffer-exhaustion risk for the performance; (7) **[[NonblockingComm|`MPI_Isend` / `MPI_Irecv`]] enable comm/compute overlap** but require the *"don't touch the buffer until completion"* contract; (8) **[[MPICommunicator|communicators]] subdivide the world into groups via the four-call `MPI_Comm_group` → `MPI_Group_incl` → `MPI_Comm_create` → `MPI_Group_rank` recipe**; (9) **debug MPI by attaching GDB** to running processes via `while (dbg) ;` + `gdb a.out <PID>` + `set var dbg = 0`; (10) **typed messages broker heterogeneity** — Intel little-endian vs Sun SPARC big-endian, 32-vs-64-bit word width — *"some of the machines literally receive the data backwards!"* if raw bytes were sent.

- New concept pages (5): [[HDFS]] (Hadoop Distributed File System — ≥3-replica fault tolerance, data locality scheduling, *"Moving computation is cheaper than moving data"*), [[HadoopStreaming]] (stdin/stdout language-agnostic interface — `key \t data` format, combiner optimization), [[WordCount]] (canonical MapReduce "Hello World" — R streaming implementation + Snowdoop implementation), [[Snowdoop]] (Matloff's pure-R MapReduce alternative — `clusterCall` + `addlists` + `Reduce`, free in-memory persistence for iterative algorithms, no fault tolerance), [[MapReduce]] (expanded from stub).

- Key takeaways: (1) **MapReduce = scatter/gather + sorting** — the shuffle phase is what distinguishes MapReduce from a plain scatter/gather; (2) **HDFS data locality** — map tasks scheduled on the node holding their input block; *"Moving computation is cheaper than moving data"*; (3) **combiner reduces network traffic** — pre-aggregates mapper output on the mapper node before the shuffle hop; (4) **Hadoop's core limitation is disk-bound iteration** — *"one cannot keep intermediate results in memory between Hadoop runs"* — iterative algorithms pay re-read cost every pass; (5) **Snowdoop trades fault tolerance for R-nativeness** — no Java, no HDFS, no configuration; uses Snow's `clusterCall` + standard `Reduce`; (6) **Snowdoop's k-means is faster for iterative algorithms** — data persists in worker RAM across iterations, *"here it comes for free, no special effort needed"*; (7) **Snowdoop's parallel I/O requires physically distributed chunks** — *"neither Hadoop, Spark nor Snowdoop will achieve full parallel reading if the file chunks are all on the same disk"*.
- Contradictions: none with prior wiki content. Ch9 consistently extends the MapReduce/Snow/scatter-gather thread from Ch1 and Ch7. The Snowdoop description of [[KMeansClustering]] is additive to the ISLR sequential description.
- Post-validation: all 5 new concept pages and 1 new entity page exist on disk; [[MapReduce]] and [[KMeansClustering]] updated in-place; source page [[wikilinks]] resolve to existing pages ([[NormMatloff]], [[UCDavis]], [[parproc-ch01-intro-parallel-processing]], [[parproc-ch07-message-passing-systems]], [[parproc-ch08-introduction-to-mpi]], [[MapReduce]], [[Hadoop]], [[HDFS]], [[HadoopStreaming]], [[WordCount]], [[Snowdoop]], [[KMeansClustering]], [[Snow]], [[ScatterGather]], [[Cluster]], [[NetworkOfWorkstations]]).
