- Key takeaways: (1) **Separation correctness is the algorithmic heart of quicksort** — `separate()` places the pivot in its final position; the sub-ranges never escape their index bounds; prefix-scan provides an alternative parallel separation. (2) **Hyperquicksort = quicksort + hypercube structure** — median broadcast + d rounds of compare-exchange on a d-cube; result is globally sorted distributed chunks without a gather step. (3) **Compare-exchange is the universal parallel sorting primitive** — bitonic mergesort, hyperquicksort, odd-even transposition, and bubble sort all reduce to variants of compare-exchange. (4) **Bubble sort is "much-maligned" serially but usable in parallel** — the inner loop is data-parallel; odd-even transposition is the regularized parallel variant. (5) **CUDA odd-even requires one kernel launch per iteration** — separate blocks cannot synchronize across a launch; pointer-swapping between primary and scratch arrays avoids write hazards. (6) **Shearsort is the canonical 2D-mesh algorithm** — snakelike output; column ops require matrix transpose via `MPI_Alltoall`. (7) **Radix sort = bucket sort with no sampling** — bit-level buckets; uniformity assumption replaces sampling; CUDPP implements via segmented scan.
- Contradictions: none with prior wiki content. Bubble sort reframe ("much-maligned serially, usable in parallel") is a new perspective not contradicting any prior page. - Source page created: `wiki/sources/parproc-ch13-audio-image-processing.md`.
- Concept pages created (5 new): [[DiscreteFourierTransform]], [[FastFourierTransform]], [[ImageSmoothing]], [[EdgeDetection]], [[FFTW]].

- Key takeaways: (1) **DFT is a Vandermonde matrix-vector product** — C = (1/n)AX; inversion exact via A(q)⁻¹ = (1/n)A(1/q); 2-D DFT separates into row+column 1-D DFTs. (2) **FFT reduces DFT from O(n²) to O(n log n)** via Cooley-Tukey divide-and-conquer; two parallel strategies: FFT recursion (mirrors Quicksort/Hyperquicksort from Ch12) vs matrix-multiply approach (preferred in shared memory). (3) **Image smoothing = low-pass filter; edge detection = high-pass filter** — both follow the same forward-DFT → coefficient zeroing → inverse-DFT pipeline. (4) **FFTW is the CPU-parallel counterpart to CUFFT** — provides OpenMP and MPI callable versions; R's fft() is serial but parApply enables 2-D parallelism. (5) **Normalization hazard** — R's `fft()` is "unnormalized"; users mixing CUFFT, FFTW, and R must reconcile 1/n vs 1/√n vs no-factor conventions.
- Contradictions: none with prior wiki content. Minor note: §13.3.2 qualifies divide-and-conquer as problematic in shared memory (thread starvation) — absent from Ch12's parallel Quicksort; consistent given FFT's shallower log₂ n recursion depth.

- Key takeaways: (1) **Apriori pruning is monotone** — support decreases under set extension, so infrequent itemsets can be pruned; inner loops embarrassingly parallel, but refinements (hash trees, large F_i) make coordination harder. (2) **KDE has convolution form** — f̂(t) = (1/nh)Σk((t−Xᵢ)/h) reduces to parallel FFT (Ch13), connecting density estimation to frequency-domain work. (3) **CUDA histograms are a bank-conflict problem** — Podlozhnyuk resolves it via per-thread (histogram64) or per-warp (histogram256) subhistograms in shared memory, merged with atomicAdd. (4) **K-means Ch14 uses Manhattan distance** — distinct from Ch9's Euclidean/Snowdoop implementation; same algorithm, different distance and framework. (5) **Monte Carlo is not trivially parallel** — C's random() gives correlated or identical streams per thread; CURAND/RngStream/SPRNG/OpenMP-MT are required.
- Contradictions: none with prior wiki content. Notable: Ch14's k-means (Snow, Manhattan distance) and Ch9's k-means (Snowdoop, Euclidean distance) are two distinct parallel implementations of the same algorithm — not contradictory, but users should not conflate them.

- Source: `https://diveintosystems.org/book/C2-C_depth/advanced_voidstar.html` → `wiki/sources/dis-2-9-3-voidstar.md`. **Third subsection of [[dis-2-9-advanced|Ch 2.9]]** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]*; finally delivers the [[VoidPointer|`void *`]] type-erased pointer that [[dis-2-2-pointers|Ch 2.2]] named-and-deferred and that [[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory|Ch 2.4]] silently relied on as [[Malloc|`malloc`]]'s return type.
- New concept pages (4): [[VoidPointer]] (the type-erased pointer with the size-uniformity rationale and the two canonical use cases: [[Malloc|`malloc`]] return type, [[Pthreads|pthread]] thread-main args), [[TypeCast]] (the `(T *)e` recast mechanism with the double-parens `*((T *)vp)` idiom), [[GenericPointer]] (the design pattern naming the *type-erased programming* approach with three canonical uses — generic return type / generic parameter / generic storage), [[Memcpy]] (`void *memcpy(void *dest, const void *src, size_t n)` named-and-deferred as a `void *`-bearing routine; three rules — no overlap, caller owns dest size, byte-level no type interpretation).
- Resolves the [[dis-2-2-pointers|Ch 2.2]] *"`void *` deferred to later Ch 2 sections"* promise. Explains the mechanism Ch 2.4's [[Malloc|`malloc`]] signature exposed without justification.
- Headline rule: **size-uniformity** — all pointer variables have the same width on a given platform (4 bytes on 32-bit, 8 on 64-bit), so the compiler can allocate `void *` storage without knowing the pointee type. The pointee's `sizeof` is irrelevant to the pointer-variable's storage size.
- Headline discipline: **recast before dereference** — `*vp` is a type error; programmer must supply `(type *)vp` first; idiomatic form is `*((int *)args)` with double parens.

These will be created when the relevant chapters (Ch 9–10 concurrency, Ch 2.9.4 pointer arithmetic) are ingested.
- Key takeaways: (1) **`void *` works because pointer width is uniform** — the architecture fixes pointer-variable storage size; pointee type only matters when interpreting the address; (2) **the cast is information the programmer supplies** — `void *` carries no pointee metadata, so the recast is the programmer's *"trust me, this is what's at that address"* assertion to the compiler; (3) **two canonical use cases** in Ch 2.9.3 — `malloc` (generic *return*) and pthread thread main (generic *parameter*); a third — generic *storage* in containers — is implicit in broader corpus; (4) **the bargain** is compile-time type-checking ↔ runtime flexibility; (5) **`void` vs `void *`** are fundamentally different — `void` is a non-type, `void *` is a real pointer type. The `*` changes everything.
- Contradictions: none. Ch 2.9.3 is purely additive — it *explains* the mechanism [[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory|Ch 2.4]]'s [[Malloc|`malloc`]] signature already exposed, and resolves the `void *` deferral [[dis-2-2-pointers|Ch 2.2]] flagged. ## [2026-05-17] ingest | Dive into Systems — Ch 4.6 Bitwise Operators

- Source: https://diveintosystems.org/book/C4-Binary/bitwise.html — [[dis-4-6-bitwise]] — the **operator-surface section** of [[DiveIntoSystems]] Ch 4 *Binary and Data Representation* that exposes [[CLanguage|C]]'s six [[BitwiseOperator|bitwise operators]] (`&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, `<<`, `>>`) as the per-bit instantiation of [[LogicGate|logic gates]].
- Headline thesis: *"bitwise operators directly apply logic gate behavior to bit sequences"* — they are the per-bit primitives executing in one clock cycle with no carry propagation, the cheapest ops in the [[InstructionSetArchitecture|ISA]]. Bridges Ch 4.1–4.5's value-level integer arithmetic into the **bit-manipulation idioms** real systems code uses (bit-test / set / clear / toggle / mask / pack).
- Six operators codified: [[BitwiseAnd|`&`]] (masking — `26 & 54 = 18`); [[BitwiseOr|`|`]] (bit-setting — `26 | 54 = 62`); [[BitwiseXor|`^`]] (toggling / equality-test — `26 ^ 54 = 44`); [[BitwiseNot|`~`]] (bit-flip — `~26 = -27` because *"bitwise NOT only flips the bits and doesn't add one"* — the `~x = -x - 1` identity under [[TwosComplement|two's complement]]); **left shift `<<`** (zero-fill, truncate at MSB — `13 << 3 = 104`, multiplication by $2^N$); **right shift `>>`** — split by operand type: [[LogicalRightShift|logical]] (unsigned → zero-fill — `0xFF000000 >> 12 = 0x000FF000`) vs. [[ArithmeticRightShift|arithmetic]] (signed → replicate [[SignBit|sign bit]] — `0xFF000000 >> 12 = 0xFFFFF000`), *"the C compiler automatically selects the appropriate shifting variant based on variable declaration."*
- Headline category warning: *"programmers often confuse the bitwise `&&` and `||` operators with `&` and `|` operators"* — the [[LogicalOperator|logical operators]] short-circuit on truth values, the bitwise ones act per bit on the operand width.
- **Closes the [[dis-4-4-3-mult-div|Ch 4.4.3]]-deferred *bit-shift power-of-two shortcut*** for multiplication and division (`x * 16 = x << 4`; `x / 16 = x >> 4` unsigned) — the **strength-reduction** pattern compilers apply automatically; survives in hand-tuned code on platforms with slow `MUL` / `DIV` (e.g., [[ARMCortexM|Cortex-M0]] has no hardware divide).
- **2 new concept pages**: [[BitwiseOperator]] (umbrella for `&` / `|` / `^` / `~` with truth tables, canonical idioms, and hardware mapping to x86 `AND` / `OR` / `XOR` / `NOT` and ARM `AND` / `ORR` / `EOR` / `MVN`) + [[BitShift]] (umbrella for `<<` / `>>` with the [[LogicalRightShift|logical]] / [[ArithmeticRightShift|arithmetic]] right-shift split, the power-of-two multiplication / division shortcut, and the [[UndefinedBehavior|UB]] pitfalls — shift-by-≥-width, signed-shift-overflow, negative shift count).

## [2026-05-17] ingest | Dive into Systems — Ch 4.7 Integer Byte Order

- Source: https://diveintosystems.org/book/C4-Binary/byte_order.html → [[dis-4-7-byte-order]].
- Ch 4.7 *Integer Byte Order* — **closes Ch 4 *Binary and Data Representation***. The **memory-layout section** codifying [[ByteOrder|byte order]] / [[Endianness|endianness]] as the convention by which a multibyte value's [[Byte|bytes]] are laid out across consecutive [[MemoryAddress|memory addresses]]. *"Byte order, sometimes referred to as endianness, describes the order in which the bytes of a multibyte value are ordered in memory."* Single-byte values have no endianness — the question is only meaningful for values wider than one byte.
- Two conventions codified: **[[BigEndian|big-endian]]** (MSByte at lowest address — matches written-numeral left-to-right reading order; [[PowerPC]] / [[SPARC]] / [[Motorola68k]] / mainframes / network protocols / [[JavaVirtualMachine|JVM]] internals) and **[[LittleEndian|little-endian]]** (LSByte at lowest address — reversed from written numerals; [[X86]] / [[X86_64]] / [[ARM]] / [[RISCV|RISC-V]] — universal in modern deployed CPUs as of 2025).
- Detection demonstrated via the [[CCast|`char *` cast]] over `int value = 0xAABBCCDD;` walking `p[0..3]` — on x86 / x86-64 the bytes walk out `DD CC BB AA`, proof of little-endian. The `%02hhX` format specifier renders a `signed char` as exactly two hex digits.
- **Three canonical scenarios** where endianness leaks out of the [[Abstraction|abstraction]]: (1) **network transmission** — *"the IETF defines big-endian as the [[NetworkByteOrder|network byte order]]"*, the standardization that fixes cross-host [[TCPIP|TCP/IP]] / [[UDP]] serialization; [[POSIX]] supplies [[Htonl|`htonl` / `ntohl` / `htons` / `ntohs`]] (no-ops on big-endian hosts, real byte-swaps on little-endian); (2) **binary file formats** — written on one host and read on another with different endianness yields garbage unless the format pins endianness ([[JPEG]] big, [[BMP]] / [[WAV]] / [[RIFF]] little, [[TIFF]] declares per-file via `II` / `MM` magic) or includes a [[ByteOrderMark|BOM]] ([[Unicode|UTF-16 / UTF-32]]); (3) **debugger / raw-memory inspection** — `gdb`'s [[GdbExamineMemory|`x/4xb`]], `od -tx1`, `hexdump -C` show **raw byte sequence** which reads reversed on little-endian hosts vs. the value the program holds.
- Architecture map: [[X86]] always little-endian (since [[Intel8080]] 1974); [[ARM]] / [[MIPS]] / [[PowerPC]] are technically [[BiEndian|bi-endian]] but virtually always run little-endian in deployment ([[POWER8]]+ on Linux flipped to little-endian to ease x86 porting). [[IBMZArchitecture|IBM z/Architecture]] mainframes are the last major big-endian deployment outside network protocol code paths.
- Etymology: Jonathan Swift's *[[GulliversTravels|Gulliver's Travels]]* (1726) via [[DannyCohen|Danny Cohen]]'s 1980 [[IETF]] IEN-137 memo *On Holy Wars and a Plea for Peace* — *"choose a convention and commit."*
- **4 new concept pages** (per *"Bundle if appropriate"*): [[ByteOrder]] (umbrella with full treatment), [[Endianness]] (alias-with-disambiguation pointing at [[ByteOrder]]), [[BigEndian]] (the MSByte-first convention), [[LittleEndian]] (the LSByte-first convention). The umbrella + alias + two sub-conventions structure mirrors how [[BitShift]] / [[LogicalRightShift]] / [[ArithmeticRightShift]] would naturally split — but here all four merit standalone pages because the cross-corpus references ([[NetworkByteOrder]], [[ByteSwap]], file formats, etc.) name them individually.

## [2026-05-17] ingest | DSPy Programming Overview

- Ingested https://dspy.ai/learn/programming/overview/ → `wiki/sources/dspy-programming-overview.md` (slug `dspy-programming-overview`). **Page 2 of 13** of the [[DSPy]] *Learn* documentation corpus — opens the **Programming** stage of the three-stage Programming → Evaluation → Optimization model framed by [[dspy-learn-index|the Learn index]]. Raw markdown saved to `raw/dspy-programming-overview.md` (extracted via WebFetch).
- **Framework-level thesis surfaced**: ***"DSPy is a bet on writing code instead of strings. In other words, building the right control flow is crucial."*** This is the canonical statement of DSPy's design philosophy and is now the load-bearing quote on both [[DSPy]] and the new [[DSPyProgrammingModel]] concept page.
- **Four-concerns decomposition**: the Programming Overview names the four orthogonal concerns a "conventional prompt" entangles into one non-portable string — **signature** (typed I/O), **adapter** (formatting / parsing), **module** logic (strategy, e.g. "thinking step by step" or tool use), and **manual optimization** (trial-and-error) — and maps each onto a DSPy API artifact ([[DSPySignatures]] / [[DSPyAdapters]] / [[DSPyModules]] / [[DSPyOptimizers]]). This is the page where the mapping is *defined*; it underwrites every later sub-page in the Learn section.
- **Three portability claims** committed to by the page: (1) swap LM / adapter without changing the rest of the program; (2) swap one module for another (`dspy.ChainOfThought` ↔ `dspy.ProgramOfThought`) without modifying the Signature — Signature is the **stable interface**, Module the **swappable strategy**; (3) run prompt-optimization *or* weight fine-tuning against the same program (the both-axes optimizer story already noted on [[DSPy]] and [[dspy-learn-index]]).
- **Programming-stage operationalization**: three nested sub-steps — define task → define initial pipeline → craft a handful of examples — under a "**start simple, then grow**" discipline. The recommended starting point for any new task is a single `dspy.ChainOfThought` module, with complexity added incrementally based on observation.

## [2026-05-17] ingest | DSPy Language Models

- Ingested https://dspy.ai/learn/programming/language_models/ → `wiki/sources/dspy-language-models.md` (slug `dspy-language-models`). **Page 3 of 13** of the [[DSPy]] *Learn* documentation corpus — operationalizes [[dspy-programming-overview|the Programming Overview's]] *"swap the LM without changing the rest of your logic"* portability claim into a **two-line code change**. Raw markdown saved to `raw/dspy-language-models.md` (extracted via WebFetch).
- **The `dspy.LM` universal client surfaced.** Single class wraps every supported provider behind one initializer signature — `dspy.LM('provider/model-name', api_key=..., **kwargs)` — bound to the rest of the program via thread-safe `dspy.configure(lm=...)` (global) or `with dspy.context(lm=...):` (block-local). This is the framework's *concrete* answer to the portability claim — the swap is two lines, not a refactor.
- **Upstream dependency exposed: [[LiteLLM]].** The page is explicit: *"DSPy supports dozens of LLM providers via LiteLLM."* `dspy.LM` is therefore a thin facade — provider authentication / request shaping / response parsing is LiteLLM's job; DSPy adds four framework-level capabilities on top (caching default-on, `rollout_id` deterministic cache-busting, per-call `lm.history` telemetry, `model_type="responses"` Responses-API opt-in). This is a useful refinement of the wiki's DSPy framing — the LM-agnosticism story is *grounded in LiteLLM's provider abstraction*, not freshly invented by DSPy.
- **Three deployment regimes with the same API.** Managed ([[openai|OpenAI]] / [[anthropic|Anthropic]] / [[gemini|Gemini]] / Vertex AI / [[Databricks]] / [[Anyscale]] / [[TogetherAI|Together AI]] / [[microsoft|Azure]]) / self-hosted GPU ([[SGLang]] via OpenAI-compatible endpoint) / local laptop ([[Ollama]] via `ollama_chat/...`). The OpenAI-compatible-endpoint pattern (prefix `openai/`, set `api_base`) is the catch-all escape hatch.
- **`rollout_id` reconciles reproducibility-by-default with deliberate variance.** Caching is on by default → repeated calls return identical outputs. `rollout_id=N` is part of the cache key → same `(rollout_id, temperature)` is cached but different `rollout_id` at `temperature > 0` yields a different sample. Currently supported by OpenAI / Databricks. This is the wiki's first record of a framework solving the *reproducibility-vs-sampling* tension explicitly.
- **`lm.history` is the per-call telemetry surface optimizers will replay against.** Every call records `prompt / messages / kwargs / response / outputs / usage / cost / timestamp / uuid / model / response_model / model_type` — wire-frame for cost accounting, debugging, and [[DSPyOptimizers|Optimizer]] replay.
- 1 new concept page: [[DSPyLM]] (DSPy's universal LM-client abstraction; `provider/model-name` convention; thread-safe global/block-local bind modes; thin facade over [[LiteLLM]] with four framework-level capabilities on top; spans three deployment regimes with the same API; the concrete operationalization of [[DSPyProgrammingModel|the Programming Model's]] *swap-the-LM* portability claim).
- 4 new entity pages: [[LiteLLM]] (BerriAI's open-source Python provider-abstraction SDK; the upstream dependency the page names explicitly), [[Ollama]] (local-laptop LLM runtime), [[SGLang]] (self-hosted-GPU inference server explicitly recommended by the page for *"accurate open models"*), [[TogetherAI]] (managed-API LLM inference provider — `together_ai/...` model string).

## [2026-05-17] ingest | DSPy Signatures

- Ingested https://dspy.ai/learn/programming/signatures/ → `wiki/sources/dspy-signatures.md` (slug `dspy-signatures`). **Page 4 of 13** of the [[DSPy]] *Learn* documentation corpus — **defines** the first of the four orthogonal artifacts [[DSPyProgrammingModel|the Programming Model]] factors out of a conventional prompt: the **Signature**. Raw markdown saved to `raw/dspy-signatures.md` (extracted via WebFetch).
- **The Signature abstraction defined.** *"A signature is a declarative specification of input/output behavior of a DSPy module"* — runtime program object, not documentation convention; field names carry semantic weight (*"a `question` differs fundamentally from an `answer`"*); the stable interface that survives [[DSPyModules|Module]] / [[DSPyAdapters|Adapter]] / [[DSPyLM|LM]] swaps.
- **Two equivalent surface forms.** **Inline** strings (`"question -> answer"`, `"context: list[str], question: str -> answer: str"` for RAG QA, `"question, choices: list[str] -> reasoning: str, selection: int"` for multi-output) optionally paired with `instructions=` kwarg for top-level guidance; and **class-based** (`class Emotion(dspy.Signature)`) which carries three things the inline form cannot — task-description docstring, `dspy.InputField(desc=...)` input hints, `dspy.OutputField(desc=...)` output constraints.
- **Five-tier type system.** Basic Python (`str` / `int` / `bool`), `typing` composites (`list[str]` / `dict[str, int]` / `Optional[float]` / `Union[str, int]`), arbitrary pydantic models (`class QueryResult(pydantic.BaseModel)` → `dspy.Signature("query: str -> result: QueryResult")`), dot-notation nested types (`MyContainer.Query`), DSPy-special types (`dspy.Image` for multi-modal input via `dspy.Image.from_url(...)`, `dspy.History` for conversational context). `typing.Literal[...]` named as the DSPy-idiomatic closed-set-classification primitive (the `Emotion` example).
- **Type-checking is warn-not-fail.** Input field values validated against type annotations at call time; mismatches trigger warnings, not exceptions; can be disabled globally via `dspy.configure(warn_on_type_mismatch=False)`. Consistent with DSPy's prototyping-first discipline.
- **Modules expand signatures under the hood.** Most consequential implementation note: *"Many DSPy modules expand signatures under the hood. For example, `dspy.ChainOfThought` adds a `reasoning` field."* A user-declared `'document -> summary'` signature passed to `dspy.ChainOfThought` acquires a `response.reasoning` slot the user never declared — the mechanism that licenses [[DSPyProgrammingModel|the Programming Model's]] *"swap one module for another without modifying the signature"* portability claim.
- **Five worked examples on the page.** (A) `'sentence -> sentiment: bool'` → `dspy.Predict` (inline, bool output); (B) `'document -> summary'` → `dspy.ChainOfThought` (signature expanded with `reasoning`); (C) `class Emotion(dspy.Signature)` with `Literal[...]` → `dspy.Predict` (closed-set classification); (D) `class CheckCitationFaithfulness(dspy.Signature)` with `desc=` hints + `dict[str, list[str]]` output → `dspy.ChainOfThought` (worked instance of a Signature acting as a verifier / metric); (E) `class DogPictureSignature(dspy.Signature)` with `image_1: dspy.Image` → `dspy.Predict` (multi-modal input).
- **Closing framing claim.** *"While signatures streamline prototyping with structured inputs/outputs, their primary value emerges when composing multiple signatures into larger DSPy modules and compiling these into optimized prompts and finetunings."* Positions Signatures as the **stable interface layer** that [[DSPyModules|Modules]] compose and [[DSPyOptimizers|Optimizers]] tune against — the API-level form of [[DSPyProgrammingModel|the Programming Model's]] *Signature-is-the-stable-interface, Module-is-the-swappable-strategy* point.
- 1 new concept page: [[DSPySignatures]] (DSPy's declarative input/output specification; inline / class-based duality; five-tier type system; warn-not-fail type checking; modules expand signatures under the hood; the **stable interface** the rest of DSPy composes against; **closes the long-standing forward reference** carried by [[DSPy]] / [[DSPyProgrammingModel]] / [[DSPyLM]] / [[dspy-learn-index]] / [[dspy-programming-overview]] / [[dspy-language-models]] since the DSPy corpus opened on 2026-05-17).

## [2026-05-17] ingest | Dive into Systems — Ch 7.4.2 If Statements in Assembly (x86-64)

- Source: `https://diveintosystems.org/book/C7-x86_64/if_statements.html` → `wiki/sources/dis-7-4-2-x86-64-if-statements.md`.
- **68th ingested DIS chapter** — second leaf of [[dis-7-4-x86-64-conditional-loops|Ch 7.4]] *Conditional Control and Loops (x86-64)*, after [[dis-7-4-1-x86-64-preliminaries|Ch 7.4.1]] *Preliminaries* and before Ch 7.4.3 *Loops*.
- Coverage: operationalizes the [[X86FlagsRegister|FLAGS]] / [[CmpInstruction|`cmp`]] / [[X86JumpInstructions|conditional-jump]] vocabulary from [[dis-7-4-1-x86-64-preliminaries|Ch 7.4.1]] into the **canonical if-then-else compilation pattern** via a single worked `getSmallest(int x, int y)` example traced through (1) **unoptimized branch-based** assembly (`cmp` + `jle` + then-branch fall-through + `jmp` to join + labeled else-branch — diamond with source condition **negated** so the jump skips the then-branch) and (2) **`-O1`-optimized branch-free** assembly (`cmp` + tentative `mov` of one arm + [[X86ConditionalMove|`cmovle`]] overwrite — three branchless instructions, `%rip` never redirected). Headline rules: *"a standard if statement [is] where a jump occurs when conditions are **not** true"*; *"when both branches of an if-else statement simply assign different values to a single variable, the compiler may use `cmov` to remove the branch entirely"*; *"the compiler takes the safe road and uses jumps"* whenever pre-evaluating both arms could fault or have side effects ([[NullPointerSafety|null-pointer]] caveat). The `cmov` family mirrors the [[X86JumpInstructions|conditional-jump family]] one-to-one (twelve named variants — signed `cmove`/`cmovne`/`cmovs`/`cmovns`/`cmovg`/`cmovge`/`cmovl`/`cmovle`; unsigned `cmova`/`cmovae`/`cmovb`/`cmovbe`).

## [2026-05-17] ingest | DSPy Evaluation Overview

- Source: `https://dspy.ai/learn/evaluation/overview/` → `raw/dspy-evaluation-overview.md` → `wiki/sources/dspy-evaluation-overview.md`.
- **Page 9 of 13** of the [[DSPy]] *Learn* documentation; **opens the Evaluation stage** of the [[dspy-learn-index|three-stage Programming → Evaluation → Optimization]] model — the first page outside the Programming stage. The Programming stage (pages 2–8) defined *how to express* a DSPy program ([[DSPySignatures|Signatures]] / [[DSPyModules|Modules]] / [[DSPyAdapters|Adapters]] / [[DSPyTools|Tools]] / [[ModelContextProtocol|MCP]] under the [[DSPyProgrammingModel|Programming Model]]); this page defines *how to measure* one before any [[DSPyOptimizers|optimization]] is attempted.
- Coverage: the **four-step iterative-evaluation loop** — (1) **collect a development set** of 20–200 worked examples — *"Even 20 input examples of your task can be useful, though 200 goes a long way"* — from four ranked sourcing options (adjacent public datasets like [[HuggingFace]] or StackExchange → permissive-license re-use → manual labeling → deployed-demo collection); (2) **define a DSPy metric** as a callable `(example, prediction) -> score` — scalar `accuracy` for simple tasks, a *"smaller DSPy program that checks multiple properties of the output"* for long-form tasks (DSPy's structural operationalization of the [[llmasjudge|LLM-as-judge]] pattern); (3) **run development evaluations** to produce a **numerical baseline** + a **qualitative diagnostic** — *"This will probably allow you to spot any major issues, and it will define a baseline for your next steps"* — the diagnostic may force a return to Programming rather than proceed forward; (4) **(recursive) optimize the metric itself** when the metric is a DSPy program — *"If your metric is itself a DSPy program, a powerful way to iterate is to optimize your metric itself. That's usually easy because the output of the metric is usually a simple value (e.g., a score out of 5)"* — a recursive-self-improvement claim structurally novel relative to other LLM-evaluation frameworks the wiki has recorded.
- Three load-bearing commitments distinguish DSPy Evaluation from generic ML evaluation: **small dev sets are sufficient** (20-example floor lowers start-up cost; 200-example ceiling marks the *"goes a long way"* point of diminishing returns for dev-set-scale work — Evaluation is **diagnostic**, not training); **intermediate-step labels are almost never needed** (*"You almost never need labels for the intermediate steps in your program in DSPy"* — the metric scores **final outputs only**; intermediate-step quality, e.g. the `reasoning` from [[ChainOfThought|`dspy.ChainOfThought`]] or the `trajectory` from [[react|`dspy.ReAct`]], is the [[DSPyOptimizers|Optimizer's]] job to discover — DSPy's structural answer to the **intermediate-supervision problem** in chain-of-thought training); **the metric is itself iterative** (*"Invest in defining metrics and improving them incrementally over time; it's hard to consistently improve what you aren't able to define"* — the [[DSPyProgrammingModel|"start simple, then grow"]] discipline from page 2 restated at the metric layer; the metric has versions over the project's lifetime).

- Source: `https://diveintosystems.org/book/C8-IA32/basics.html` → `wiki/sources/dis-8-1-ia32-basics.md`.
- **First leaf of Ch 8 *32-bit IA32 Assembly***, the **32-bit structural twin of [[dis-7-1-x86-64-basics|Ch 7.1]]**. - **Four headline 32-vs-64 deltas** drive the ingest: (1) **eight** [[GeneralPurposeRegister|GPRs]] (`%eax`/`%ebx`/`%ecx`/`%edx`/`%edi`/`%esi`/`%esp`/`%ebp`) vs Ch 7.1's 16 (no `%r8`–`%r15`); (2) **letter-substitution subregisters only** (`%eax` → `%ax` → `%al`/`%ah`) — the suffix scheme `%r8` → `%r8d` only exists in [[X86_64|x86-64]]; (3) **stack-based parameter passing** ([[CdeclCallingConvention|cdecl]]) — IA32 has **no** [[SystemVCallingConvention|System V six-argument-register]] convention; all args pushed on stack, accessed inside the callee as `8(%ebp)`, `12(%ebp)`, `16(%ebp)`, ... ; (4) **`l` is the default integer width** (32 bits) — the 64-bit `q` suffix has no IA32 application.
- The [[Operand|operand-type]] taxonomy, [[X86AddressingMode|`disp(base, index, scale)` addressing modes]] (with `scale ∈ {1,2,4,8}`), and [[AtAndTSyntax|source-then-destination AT&T order]] are **structurally identical** to [[dis-7-1-x86-64-basics|Ch 7.1]] — the per-instruction interface is a CISC-family invariant, not register-width-dependent.
- New concept page (1): [[CdeclCallingConvention]] — the IA32 cdecl ABI codified as the headline delta from [[SystemVCallingConvention|System V AMD64]]: all args on stack, caller cleanup, return value in `%eax` (or `%edx:%eax` for 64-bit), caller-saved `%eax`/`%ecx`/`%edx` vs callee-saved `%ebx`/`%esi`/`%edi`/`%ebp`. Caller cleanup is what makes cdecl naturally variadic-compatible ([[Printf|`printf`]], [[Scanf|`scanf`]]).

- **No new concept pages.** Reuses [[CallInstruction]] / [[RetInstruction]] / [[LeaveInstruction]] / [[CallingConvention]] / [[CdeclCallingConvention]] / [[StackPointer]] / [[FramePointer]] / [[CallerSavedRegister]] / [[CalleeSavedRegister]] from [[dis-7-5-x86-64-functions|Ch 7.5]] + [[dis-8-1-ia32-basics|Ch 8.1]].

Shows how the [[CLanguage|C]] [[CStruct|struct]] composite type compiles at IA32 width: fields stored contiguously in declaration order, accessed via fixed byte-offsets (`disp(base)` addressing). **88th ingested DIS chapter.**
- Headline 32-vs-64 deltas: (1) [[AlignmentRule|alignment policy]] **caps at 4 bytes** — *"two-byte data types reside at a two-byte-aligned address whereas four-byte data types reside at four-byte-aligned addresses"* — vs Ch 7.9's 8-byte alignment for `double`/`long long`/pointer; (2) pointer fields 4 bytes wide and 4-byte-aligned (vs 8/8); (3) [[StructPadding|padding]] typically smaller — a rare case where IA32 is more space-efficient than x86-64 at the per-struct level. Field-reordering minimizes wasted space.
- **No new concept pages.** Reuses [[StructLayout]] / [[StructPadding]] / [[AlignmentRule]] / [[CStruct]] / [[X86AddressingMode]] from [[dis-7-9-x86-64-structs|Ch 7.9]].

- Headline 32-vs-64 deltas: (1) saved-return-address is 4 bytes wide (exploit payloads use 4-byte little-endian address strings, not 8-byte); (2) smaller buffer-to-saved-return-address distance per 4-byte stack-word stride; (3) attack mechanism, three-defense taxonomy ([[StackCanary]] / [[AddressSpaceLayoutRandomization|ASLR]] / [[ExecutableSpaceProtection|NX/W^X]]) and [[ReturnOrientedProgramming|ROP]] bypass are **structurally identical** to Ch 7.10. **Root cause** *"C does not perform automatic array bounds checking"* is ISA-independent.
- **No new concept pages.** Reuses [[BufferOverflow]] / [[StackSmashing]] / [[ReturnAddressOverwrite]] / [[StackCanary]] / [[AddressSpaceLayoutRandomization]] / [[ExecutableSpaceProtection]] / [[ReturnOrientedProgramming]] from [[dis-7-10-x86-64-buffer-overflow|Ch 7.10]].

## [2026-05-17] ingest | Dive into Systems — Ch 13.1 Booting and Running the OS
- **Source**: `https://diveintosystems.org/book/C13-OS/impl.html` → `wiki/sources/dis-13-1-booting-running.md`.
- **Summary**: Opening leaf of Ch 13 *The Operating System*; pivots Part V (OS-implementation arc) from Part IV (performance-tuning). Codifies how the OS starts ([[Firmware]] [[BIOS]] / [[UEFI]] loads [[Bootloader|boot block]] from disk → CPU jumps), how it launches user programs (allocate RAM → load binary → create [[Process]] state → initialize CPU), and the **interrupt-driven architecture** (OS sleeps until hardware or user program signals). Codifies the **dual-mode CPU** ([[KernelMode]] vs [[UserMode]]) and the **[[SystemCall]] trap** as the controlled mode-switch gateway: user places syscall # in an ISA-specific register and issues a trap; CPU switches privilege, runs OS handler, returns to user mode at the instruction after the trap. **Two interrupt sources**: hardware (device interrupt bus) and software (traps). **Kernel-in-every-address-space optimization** makes [[ContextSwitch|context switching]] cheap; Meltdown later forced stricter kernel-user memory separation.
- **New concept pages**: [[Bootloader]], [[Kernel]], [[KernelMode]], [[UserMode]], [[SystemCall]] (5 new).
- **Extended in-place**: [[Interrupt]] (added OS-level interrupt-driven framing + trap/hardware two-source split), [[ContextSwitch]] (added mode-switch flavor + kernel-in-every-address-space optimization + Meltdown note).

- **Source**: `https://diveintosystems.org/book/C14-SharedMemory/cache_coherence.html` → `wiki/sources/dis-14-5-cache-coherence.md`.
- **Summary**: Fifth leaf of Ch 14; pivots from [[dis-14-4-performance|Ch 14.4]]'s performance theory into hardware-level subtlety. Codifies [[SnoopingProtocol|snoopy caches]] monitoring the [[MemoryBus|memory bus]] + write-invalidate [[MESI|MESI]]-family protocols — *"every write to counts invalidates the entire line in every other L1 cache"*. **Headline failure mode**: [[FalseSharing|false sharing]] — writes to different array elements on the same [[CacheLine|cache line]] trigger invalidations even without true sharing. **Measured pathology**: per-thread counter array slows **0.34 s → 0.80 s → 0.77 s** going 1→2→4 threads — opposite of [[ParallelSpeedup|speedup]]. Mitigations: thread-local accumulators + cache-line padding.

- **Position**: third wiki-corpus [[DSPy]] tutorial (after [[dspy-conversation-history]] and [[dspy-customer-service-agent]]); first to anchor on the custom `class MyProgram(dspy.Module)` shape itself rather than on a downstream application. Template-level anchor for **rung 2** of the [[DSPy]] application stack — the canonical worked starting receipt every other rung composes from.
- **Headline**: four positions — (1) subclass `dspy.Module` and implement `__init__` + `forward`; (2) `forward()` is unconstrained Python (Langchain / Agno / MCP / database handlers compose freely inside); (3) call the module instance directly, not `forward()` explicitly (`__call__` is the trace point for [[DSPyOptimizers|optimizer]] replay + [[MLflow]] auto-logging + [[DSPyHistory|history]] threading + `Prediction.get_lm_usage()` accounting); (4) custom modules unlock framework features ([[DSPyOptimizers|DSPy Optimizer]] introspection + [[MLflow]] tracing both walk `self.*` sub-module attributes — plain-function pipelines are invisible to both).
- **Worked receipt**: three-stage [[rag|RAG]] program — `dspy.Predict(QueryGenerator)` → `dspy.ColBERTv2(url='http://20.102.90.50:2017/wiki17_abstracts')(query, k=1)` → [[chainofthought|`dspy.ChainOfThought("question,context->answer")`]]. Five load-bearing details: class-based + inline-string [[DSPySignatures|Signatures]] compose freely in the same module; retrieval is a plain Python function (optimizer can't see it); the public Wikipedia 2017 abstracts [[ColBERTv2]] endpoint is `http://20.102.90.50:2017/wiki17_abstracts`; `forward` unwraps sub-module outputs by attribute access (`.query`, `.answer`); `**kwargs` absorbs framework metadata.
- **MLflow integration**: first wiki-corpus DSPy-specific [[MLflow]] tracing recipe — four-step opt-in ending in `mlflow.dspy.autolog()` (the bridge hook that turns every `dspy.Module.__call__` into an MLflow trace span). [[Databricks]] owns [[MLflow]] — second [[Databricks]]-touchpoint in the DSPy line after [[MateiZaharia]]'s [[2406.11695-mipro|MIPRO]] / [[2507.19457-gepa|GEPA]] senior-author roles.
- **New concept page (1)**: [[ColBERTv2]] — promoted from long-standing forward reference carried by [[DSPyModules]] / [[DSPyOptimizers]] / [[DSPyPrediction]] / [[hotpotqa]] / [[BetterTogether]] / [[MIPROv2]] / [[react]] / [[chainofthought]] since the [[DSPy]] *Learn* corpus opened on 2026-05-17. - **Key concepts**: [[ComputationSpace|computation space]] (tasks + 3-compartment store: [[ConstraintStore|constraint store]] / procedure store / cell store); monotonic synchronization on **logic entailment** of guards; [[Propagator|propagators]] for nonbasic constraints; **threads** as reduction strategy (*"as sequential as possible and as concurrent as necessary"*); [[Port|ports]] / [[Agent|agents]] / [[OPMObject|objects]] as derived stateful abstractions; **search combinator** encapsulating CLP search into concurrent agents.

## [2026-05-22] ingest | LLM Engineer's Handbook — Ch 6: Fine-Tuning with Preference Alignment

Source: [[leh-ch06-preference-alignment]]
- **Headline**: introduces preference alignment as the post-SFT stage; contrasts [[rlhf|RLHF]]+PPO with [[DirectPreferenceOptimization|DPO]] (derives DPO's closed-form policy from the standard RLHF objective + KL constraint, reducing preference learning to a binary cross-entropy over chosen/rejected log-probs with a `beta`-weighted KL term).
- **New concept pages**: [[DirectPreferenceOptimization]] (canonical), [[DPO]] (alias).
- **Worked example**: builds `mlabonne/llmtwin-dpo` (1,467 filtered samples) by treating extracted article passages as **chosen** and GPT-4o-mini answers as **rejected**; DPO-fine-tunes `mlabonne/TwinLlama-3.1-8B` with Unsloth (LoRA r=32, `beta=0.5`, lr=2e-6, 1 epoch); shares weights between policy and reference via adapters (`ref_model=None` in TRL's `DPOTrainer`).
- **Concept extensions in place**: [[rlhf]] gains the PbRL prehistory (Akrour 2011, Cheng 2011) + the DPO-vs-PPO performance-ceiling nuance; [[KullbackLeiblerDivergence]] / [[RewardFunction]] / [[reinforcementlearning]] / [[ExplorationExploitation]] / [[lora]] / [[QLoRA]] / [[adapterlayers]] / [[CrossEntropyLoss]] / [[LLMAsAJudge]] / [[chainofthought]] / [[Hallucination]] / [[Adam]] / [[anthropic]] / [[openai]] / [[meta]] / [[NVIDIA]] / [[Databricks]] / [[HuggingFace]] / [[CometML]] / [[Llama3_8BInstruct]] gain in-place edits.
- **Key tuning notes**: chosen/rejected accuracy reaching 100% means the dataset is too easy; key metrics to watch are chosen/rejected reward, margin, accuracy, gradient norm, train/val loss; the `beta=0.5` choice is deliberately higher than the standard 0.1 to stay closer to SFT and avoid DPO's tendency toward overly formal/verbose output.
- **Contradictions**: none.

## [2026-05-22] ingest | LLM Engineer's Handbook — Ch 11: MLOps and LLMOps

Source: [[leh-ch11-mlops-and-llmops]]
- **Headline**: closes the book with the **DevOps → [[MLOps]] → [[LLMOps]]** hierarchy. LLMOps inherits the six MLOps principles (automation, versioning, experiment tracking, testing, monitoring, reproducibility) and adds LLM-specific concerns: prompt monitoring with full traces, input/output guardrails, RLHF/DPO feedback loops, and the recognition that most teams don't train foundation models from scratch (~$100M for GPT-4) so the operational focus is fine-tuning + prompt engineering + RAG.
- **Hands-on deployment**: provisions MongoDB Atlas (free) + Qdrant Cloud (free) + ZenML Cloud (trial) + AWS (ECR + S3 + SageMaker + IAM + CloudFormation); Dockerfile uses `python:3.11-slim-bullseye` with Google Chrome for the crawlers and `--platform linux/amd64` to bypass macOS/Windows incompatibility. Switches ZenML from local stack to `aws-stack` to run pipelines as SageMaker processing jobs.
- **CI / CD / CT topology**: CI via GitHub Actions (gitleaks → Ruff lint → Ruff format → pytest); CD on push to `main` builds + tags Docker image and pushes to ECR; CT chains data + feature + training + deploy pipelines via an `end_to_end_data` master pipeline (a self-flagged workaround for ZenML free-tier's 3-pipeline cap). Prompt tracing via Opik's `@track` decorator on `rag()` / `call_llm_service()` / `ContextRetriever.search()` / `SelfQuery.generate()`.
- **LLM latency metrics**: TTFT (Time to First Token), TBT (Time Between Tokens), TPS, TPOT, Total Latency — five distinct metrics matter because tokens stream.
- **Drift taxonomy (appendix)**: [[DataDrift]] / [[TargetDrift]] / [[ConceptDrift]] decomposition; KS-test for univariate continuous, chi-squared for categorical, MMD on reduced embeddings for text; uses `alibi_detect.cd.KSDrift` and `…MMDDrift`. **Behavioral testing** of NLP models (invariance, directional, minimum-functionality) per the [[CheckList]] paper.
- **Concept extensions in place**: [[MLOps]] / [[CICD]] / [[Monitoring]] / [[ModelMonitoring]] / [[ModelRegistry]] / [[FeatureStore]] / [[FeatureEngineering]] / [[DataDrift]] / [[TargetDrift]] / [[ConceptDrift]] / [[LabelShift]] / [[Reproducibility]] / [[ReproducibilityInML]] / [[Hallucination]] / [[Guardrail]] / [[GuardrailsAI]] / [[NeMoGuardrails]] / [[Jailbreak]] / [[promptinjection]] / [[rlhf]] / [[DPO]] / [[rag]] / [[CometML]] / [[MLflow]] / [[WeightsAndBiases]] / [[Neptune]] / [[AmazonSageMaker]] / [[GitHub]] / [[GitHubActions]] / [[FastAPI]] / [[SecretsScanning]] / [[CanaryDeployment]] / [[ShadowDeployment]] / [[DVC]] / [[GitLFS]] / [[Versioning]] / [[Testing]] / [[UnitTesting]] / [[IntegrationTesting]] / [[RegressionTesting]] / [[BehavioralTesting]] / [[CheckList]] gain in-place edits via sibling agents.
- **Notable claim**: *"An ML system can complete training successfully and silently produce wrong results — unlike traditional software, no exceptions are thrown."* This is why monitoring + behavioral tests + drift detection are non-negotiable in MLOps/LLMOps.
- **Contradictions**: none. The `end_to_end_data` master pipeline is self-flagged as an anti-pattern adopted only because of the ZenML free-tier 3-pipeline cap.

## [2026-05-23] ingest | IIR Ch. 1: Boolean Retrieval

Source: [[iir-ch01-boolean-retrieval]]
- Manning/Raghavan/Schütze 2008 — the canonical IR textbook's opening chapter. Sets up information retrieval against grep-style linear scan, motivates the [[InvertedIndex]] via the Shakespeare collection, defines the term-document incidence matrix.
- Algorithms: BUILD-INVERTED-INDEX (parse → sort by (term, docID) → merge with df counts) and INTERSECT (two-pointer merge of sorted postings, O(x+y)).
- Concept seeds: [[BooleanRetrieval]], [[TermDocumentMatrix]], [[PostingsList]], [[RankedRetrieval]] (forward-pointer to chapter 6).

## [2026-05-23] ingest | IIR Ch. 2: The Term Vocabulary and Postings Lists

Source: [[iir-ch02-term-vocabulary-postings]]
- Document delineation + character decoding (encoding, language ID, document unit choice); [[Tokenization]] decisions (hyphenation, apostrophes, CJK segmentation); stop words & their decline as compression makes them tractable; equivalence-class normalization (case folding, accent removal, asymmetric expansion); [[Stemming]] vs [[Lemmatization]] — Porter, Lovins, Paice/Husk stemmers.
- Skip pointers placed at √P intervals (sqrt-heuristic) for faster intersection; biword index for phrase queries; positional index with `(term, df; doc1: pos1, pos2, …)`; combination schemes (next-word index, common-term biwords).

## [2026-05-23] ingest | IIR Ch. 3: Dictionaries and Tolerant Retrieval

Source: [[iir-ch03-dictionaries-tolerant-retrieval]]
- Dictionary search structures: hash tables (O(1) but no prefix / range) vs B-trees (O(log n) ordered). Wildcard queries: trailing wildcards via B-tree; general wildcards via permuterm index (rotate "hello$" through all rotations) or k-gram index (intersect postings of overlapping k-grams).
- Spelling correction: edit distance via Levenshtein DP (insert/delete/substitute = 1, optionally transpose for Damerau-Levenshtein); k-gram + Jaccard for candidate generation; context-sensitive correction via co-occurrence counts; Soundex phonetic correction (consonant-class collapse).
- Concept seeds: [[Permuterm]], [[KGramIndex]], [[Levenshtein]], [[Soundex]], [[JaccardCoefficient]], [[WildcardQuery]], [[SpellingCorrection]].

## [2026-05-23] ingest | IIR Ch. 4: Index Construction

Source: [[iir-ch04-index-construction]]
- Hardware-motivated indexing: disk seek dominates cost; sequential I/O wins. BSBI (Blocked Sort-Based Indexing): parse to (term, docID), sort blocks in memory, write to disk, merge with priority queue. SPIMI (Single-Pass In-Memory Indexing): per-block dictionary + postings, append directly to postings, no global termID mapping. Reuters-RCV1: ~800K docs, ~100M tokens, ~400K terms.
- Distributed indexing via [[MapReduce]] (parsers → key-by-term-partition → inverters merge). Dynamic indexing: auxiliary in-memory index + periodic merges; logarithmic merging keeps amortized cost O(T log T / n).
- Concept seeds: [[BSBI]], [[SPIMI]], [[DistributedIndexing]], [[DynamicIndexing]], [[LogarithmicMerging]], [[ReutersRCV1]].

## [2026-05-23] ingest | IIR Ch. 5: Index Compression

Source: [[iir-ch05-index-compression]]
- Heaps' law M = k · T^b (k ≈ 30–100, b ≈ 0.49) — vocabulary grows sublinearly with collection size, never saturates. [[ZipfsLaw]] cf_i ∝ 1/i — the i-th most frequent term has frequency ∝ 1/i; both are power laws.
- Dictionary compression: dictionary-as-string saves fixed-width term-field padding; blocked storage with k-term blocks + front coding (shared prefix length + suffix). Postings file compression: variable byte codes (7 data bits + continuation bit per byte); gamma codes (unary prefix length + binary offset) → bit-aligned, smaller for small gaps.
- RCV1: dictionary 11MB → ~3MB; postings 250MB → ~100MB (γ) or ~116MB (VByte).
- Concept seeds: [[HeapsLaw]], [[FrontCoding]], [[VariableByteCode]], [[GammaCode]], [[UnaryCode]], [[DictionaryCompression]], [[PostingsCompression]].

## [2026-05-23] ingest | IIR Ch. 6: Scoring, Term Weighting and the Vector Space Model

Source: [[iir-ch06-vector-space-model]]
- Parametric & zone indexes for fielded retrieval; weighted zone scoring score = Σ_i g_i · zone_i, with weights g learnable from training data. Core weighting: tf (term frequency in doc), idf_t = log(N/df_t), tf-idf = tf · idf.
- Vector space model: documents as vectors in V-dimensional term space; cosine similarity sim(d_1, d_2) = (d_1 · d_2) / (||d_1|| ||d_2||) is length-invariant. COSINESCORE algorithm: accumulate per-doc tf-idf scores via postings traversal, length-normalize at the end. SMART notation ddd.qqq encodes (term frequency, document frequency, normalization) for documents vs queries. Pivoted length normalization corrects under-retrieval of long documents.
- Concept seeds: [[VectorSpaceModel]], [[TfIdf]], [[TermFrequency]], [[InverseDocumentFrequency]], [[ZoneIndex]], [[SmartNotation]], [[PivotedLengthNormalization]].

## [2026-05-23] ingest | IIR Ch. 7: Computing Scores in a Complete Search System

Source: [[iir-ch07-complete-search-system]]
- Efficient top-K via min-heap selection O(J log K) on J candidate documents (vs O(J log J) full sort). Inexact top-K is fine because cosine itself is a proxy for relevance: index elimination (skip low-idf query terms or docs with < t query terms); champion lists (per term, precompute top-r-by-tf-idf docs); static quality scores g(d) (PageRank, doc popularity) combined as net-score(q,d) = g(d) + cos(q,d), used to order postings; impact ordering (postings sorted by weight, early termination); cluster pruning with √N leaders and document-to-leader index.
- Components: tiered indexes (high-quality tier first, fall through to lower tiers if < K hits); query-term proximity bonuses; full query parser + scorer pipeline.
- Concept seeds: [[TopKRetrieval]], [[ChampionLists]], [[StaticQualityScore]], [[ImpactOrdering]], [[ClusterPruning]], [[TieredIndex]], [[QueryProximity]].

## [2026-05-23] ingest | IIR Ch. 8: Evaluation in Information Retrieval

Source: [[iir-ch08-ir-evaluation]]
- Cranfield paradigm = (test collection, query set, relevance judgments) → reproducible offline evaluation. TREC test collections (Reuters-21578, GOV2, ClueWeb, etc.). Unranked: precision = |relevant ∩ retrieved| / |retrieved|, recall = |relevant ∩ retrieved| / |relevant|, accuracy (≈ useless for IR — most docs are non-relevant), F_β = (β² + 1)PR / (β²P + R).
- Ranked: 11-point interpolated AP; MAP (mean over queries of AP); R-precision (precision at recall = 1); NDCG_p = Σ (2^rel_i − 1) / log_2(i+1) normalized by ideal DCG. Inter-annotator agreement via Cohen's kappa κ = (P(A) − P(E)) / (1 − P(E)).
- User-utility view: A/B testing on live systems; snippet generation for SERP UX.
- Concept seeds: [[Precision]], [[Recall]], [[FMeasure]], [[MeanAveragePrecision]], [[NDCG]], [[RPrecision]], [[KappaCoefficient]], [[TRECCollection]], [[CranfieldParadigm]].

## [2026-05-23] ingest | IIR Ch. 9: Relevance Feedback and Query Expansion

Source: [[iir-ch09-relevance-feedback-query-expansion]]
- Rocchio relevance feedback in the vector space: q_m = α q_0 + (β/|D_r|) Σ d_j∈D_r − (γ/|D_nr|) Σ d_j∈D_nr; typical α=1, β=0.75, γ=0.15. Ide dec-hi: only subtract the top non-relevant. Pseudo-relevance feedback (PRF): treat top-k as relevant blindly — fragile to topic drift. Indirect feedback via clickthrough.
- Global query reformulation: hand-built thesauri (WordNet, MeSH), automatic thesaurus via term-term co-occurrence over the corpus; expansion can hurt precision if synonyms are noisy.
- Concept seeds: [[RelevanceFeedback]], [[RocchioAlgorithm]], [[PseudoRelevanceFeedback]], [[QueryExpansion]], [[AutomaticThesaurus]], [[WordNet]], [[Clickthrough]].

## [2026-05-23] ingest | IIR Ch. 10: XML Retrieval

Source: [[iir-ch10-xml-retrieval]]
- XML data model (elements + attributes), XPath axis navigation. Structured retrieval challenges: schema diversity across collections; granularity (return whole doc vs section vs paragraph); overlap; nested elements with different scoring. Structural-term / lexicalized-subtree index combines content with structural context.
- Context-resemblance similarity sim(c_q, c_d) weights match by structural compatibility. INEX benchmark; NEXI query language (XPath subset for retrieval). Text-centric (literature, articles — flexible structure) vs data-centric (transactional records — rigid).
- Concept seeds: [[XMLRetrieval]], [[XPath]], [[StructuralTerm]], [[NEXI]], [[SchemaDiversity]], [[XQuery]].
- Entity seeds: [[W3C]], [[INEX]].

## [2026-05-23] ingest | IIR Ch. 11: Probabilistic Information Retrieval

Source: [[iir-ch11-probabilistic-ir]]
- Probability Ranking Principle (Robertson 1977): rank docs by P(R=1|q,d) is optimal under 1/0 loss. Binary Independence Model assumes term independence given relevance + binary occurrence. Derives Retrieval Status Value RSV_d = Σ_{t∈q∩d} log[p_t(1−u_t) / (u_t(1−p_t))] where p_t = P(t|R=1), u_t = P(t|R=0).
- Probability estimation: theoretical via known relevance set; in practice u_t ≈ df_t / N when R is unknown; smoothing with add-1/2.
- Extensions: tree-structured dependencies; Okapi [[BM25]] = non-binary extension with tf saturation k_1 and length normalization b; Bayesian network IR. BM25 is the chapter's modern legacy — the workhorse of pre-neural retrieval.
- Concept seeds: [[ProbabilityRankingPrinciple]], [[BinaryIndependenceModel]], [[RetrievalStatusValue]], [[OkapiBM25]], [[BayesianNetwork]].

## [2026-05-23] ingest | IIR Ch. 12: Language Models for Information Retrieval

Source: [[iir-ch12-language-models-ir]]
- 2008-era *statistical* language models — NOT modern neural LMs. Finite automata view; unigram / bigram / n-gram LMs; multinomial distribution over vocabulary. Query likelihood: rank docs by P(q | M_d), with multinomial unigram M_d estimated from doc.
- Smoothing is essential: Jelinek-Mercer P(t|d) = λ P_mle(t|M_d) + (1−λ) P_mle(t|M_c); Dirichlet P(t|d) = (tf_t,d + μ P(t|M_c)) / (L_d + μ). Ponte & Croft 1998 — first IR application of LMs. Equivalent to log-linear models / vector-space scoring under specific term-weighting choices.
- Concept seeds: [[QueryLikelihoodModel]], [[StatisticalLanguageModel]], [[JelinekMercerSmoothing]], [[DirichletSmoothing]], [[FiniteStateAutomaton]], [[Multinomial]].

## [2026-05-23] ingest | IIR Ch. 13: Text Classification and Naive Bayes

Source: [[iir-ch13-text-classification-naive-bayes]]
- Multinomial vs Bernoulli NB: multinomial models token positions, P(d|c) = Π P(t|c)^{n_t,d}; Bernoulli models binary term occurrence, P(d|c) = Π P(t|c)^{x_t} (1−P(t|c))^{1−x_t}. MAP with [[LaplaceSmoothing]] avoids zero probabilities.
- Feature selection: [[MutualInformation]] I(U;C) = ΣΣ P(U,C) log [P(U,C) / (P(U)P(C))]; chi-square X²(t,c) = Σ (O−E)²/E; frequency-based. Micro-averaged F1 (pool TP/FP/FN) vs macro-averaged (mean over classes — favors rare classes). Reuters-21578 ModApte split is the canonical benchmark.
- Concept seeds: [[MultinomialNaiveBayes]], [[BernoulliNaiveBayes]], [[FeatureSelection]], [[MicroAveraging]], [[MacroAveraging]], [[Reuters21578]].
- Entity seeds: [[ThomasBayes]].

## [2026-05-23] ingest | IIR Ch. 14: Vector Space Classification

Source: [[iir-ch14-vector-space-classification]]
- Rocchio classification: train one centroid per class via μ_c = (1/|D_c|) Σ d∈D_c; classify by nearest centroid (cosine). Convex but cannot represent multi-modal classes.
- k-Nearest Neighbor: classify by majority (or distance-weighted) class among the k nearest training docs. Voronoi tessellation = decision regions for k=1. Time complexity O(|D| · M_a) test-time (each test doc compared to every training doc) — prohibitive at scale without indexing.
- Linear vs nonlinear classifiers; one-vs-rest for multiclass; any-of (multi-label) vs one-of. Bias-variance decomposition E[(γ̂(d) − γ(d))²] = bias² + variance — high-bias classifiers (NB, Rocchio) vs high-variance (kNN with small k).
- Concept seeds: [[RocchioClassification]], [[KNearestNeighbor]], [[VoronoiTessellation]], [[LinearClassifier]], [[OneVsRest]], [[BiasVarianceTradeoff]].

## [2026-05-23] ingest | IIR Ch. 15: Support Vector Machines and Machine Learning on Documents

Source: [[iir-ch15-svm-ml-on-documents]]
- Linearly separable case: maximize margin 2/||w|| subject to y_i(w·x_i + b) ≥ 1 → quadratic program. Lagrangian dual yields support vectors (α_i > 0 for boundary points only). Soft margin with slack ξ_i: minimize ½||w||² + C Σ ξ_i for non-separable data. Kernel trick: replace inner product with K(x_i, x_j), e.g. polynomial (1 + x_i·x_j)^d, RBF exp(−γ||x_i − x_j||²).
- Multiclass via one-vs-rest or structural SVMs (joint feature space, ranking loss). Learning-to-rank: pairwise loss (RankingSVM minimizes pairwise inversions), pointwise, listwise. Text-classification considerations: feature selection, document zones, hierarchical taxonomies.
- Concept seeds: [[SupportVectorMachine]], [[MaximumMargin]], [[SoftMargin]], [[KernelTrick]], [[RBFKernel]], [[StructuralSVM]], [[LearningToRank]], [[RankingSVM]].
- Entity seeds: [[VladimirVapnik]], [[ThorstenJoachims]].

## [2026-05-23] ingest | IIR Ch. 16: Flat Clustering

Source: [[iir-ch16-flat-clustering]]
- Cluster hypothesis: documents in the same cluster behave similarly with respect to relevance to queries — the foundation for cluster-based retrieval. Partitional vs hierarchical; hard vs soft.
- K-means (Lloyd's algorithm): initialize K centroids; iterate (1) assign each doc to nearest centroid, (2) recompute centroids. Monotonically decreases RSS = Σ_k Σ_d∈ω_k ||d − μ_k||². Choose K via elbow on RSS, AIC, BIC.
- Model-based clustering with EM: maximize log-likelihood under a mixture model; soft assignments via E-step posteriors. External evaluation: purity (max-class fraction per cluster, averaged), NMI = I(Ω;C) / [(H(Ω) + H(C))/2], Rand Index, F-measure for clustering.
- Concept seeds: [[ClusterHypothesis]], [[FlatClustering]], [[EMAlgorithm]], [[Purity]], [[NormalizedMutualInformation]], [[RandIndex]], [[ModelBasedClustering]].

## [2026-05-23] ingest | IIR Ch. 17: Hierarchical Clustering

Source: [[iir-ch17-hierarchical-clustering]]
- HAC (Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering): start with N singletons, repeatedly merge the two closest, build a dendrogram. With priority queue: O(N² log N). Linkage criteria differ in how cluster-to-cluster distance is defined: single-link (min — chaining effect, elongated clusters), complete-link (max — compact but sensitive to outliers), group-average (mean over all pairs), centroid-link (distance between centroids — non-monotonic, inversions possible).
- Divisive (top-down) clustering: bisecting K-means recursively. Cluster labeling via differential test (terms enriched inside cluster vs outside).
- Concept seeds: [[HAC]], [[SingleLinkClustering]], [[CompleteLinkClustering]], [[GroupAverageClustering]], [[DivisiveClustering]], [[BisectingKMeans]], [[ClusterLabeling]].

## [2026-05-23] ingest | IIR Ch. 18: Matrix Decompositions and Latent Semantic Indexing

Source: [[iir-ch18-lsi-matrix-decompositions]]
- Linear algebra review: eigendecomposition A = QΛQ^{-1} (square), symmetric A = QΛQ^T (orthogonal Q). SVD generalizes to rectangular C = UΣV^T (U, V orthonormal, Σ diagonal of singular values).
- Truncated SVD C_k = U_k Σ_k V_k^T (top k singular triples) is the best rank-k approximation in Frobenius norm (Eckart-Young theorem) — minimum ||C − C_k||_F². LSI applies truncated SVD to the term-document matrix to project queries/docs into a k-dim "concept" space, partially handling synonymy (different terms project near same concept) and polysemy (same term spreads across concepts).
- Query folding: q_k = Σ_k^{-1} U_k^T q maps a query into the latent space. LSI = LSA outside the IR context.
- Concept seeds: [[LatentSemanticIndexing]], [[LatentSemanticAnalysis]], [[SingularValueDecomposition]], [[LowRankApproximation]], [[EckartYoungTheorem]], [[FrobeniusNorm]], [[Synonymy]], [[Polysemy]].
- Entity seeds: [[SusanDumais]], [[ScottDeerwester]].

## [2026-05-23] ingest | IIR Ch. 19: Web Search Basics

Source: [[iir-ch19-web-search-basics]]
- Pre-Google search: Altavista, Yahoo directory, Inktomi. Bow-tie web graph (Broder et al. 2000): SCC core (~30%), IN (links to SCC), OUT (linked from SCC), tendrils, disconnected components. Spam: keyword stuffing, cloaking, doorway pages, link farms — adversarial IR.
- Economic model: paid placement (CPC, CPM, CPA) auctions; algorithmic results separate from ads. Broder's query intent taxonomy: informational (find facts), navigational (go to a known site), transactional (buy/download/interact).
- Index size estimation via capture-recapture: |index_A ∩ index_B| / |index_B| ≈ |sample_A| / |Web|. Near-duplicate detection via shingling: each doc = set of k-shingles (k-gram of words); Jaccard similarity J(A,B) = |A∩B|/|A∪B| estimated cheaply by min-hash sketches (random permutation π → minhash(A) = min_{x∈A} π(x); P[minhash(A) = minhash(B)] = J(A,B)).
- Concept seeds: [[WebGraph]], [[BowTie]], [[WebSpam]], [[Cloaking]], [[PaidPlacement]], [[CostPerClick]], [[QueryIntent]], [[NavigationalQuery]], [[InformationalQuery]], [[TransactionalQuery]], [[Shingling]], [[MinHash]], [[NearDuplicateDetection]].

## [2026-05-23] ingest | IIR Ch. 20: Web Crawling and Indexes

Source: [[iir-ch20-web-crawling-indexes]]
- Crawler requirements: politeness (respect robots.txt + per-host rate limits), freshness, scalability, distributed operation, extensibility. Mercator-style architecture: URL frontier with front queues (priority/freshness) feeding back queues (one per host) feeding a heap of next-fetch times for politeness scheduling.
- DNS is the surprise bottleneck — synchronous resolution serializes; production crawlers use async DNS + caching. Duplicate elimination via content hashes (Rabin fingerprints) on document body. Sitemaps protocol for hint-driven crawling.
- Distributed indexes: term-partitioned (one term's full postings on one shard — low total work, hot terms imbalance) vs document-partitioned (each shard indexes a doc range — symmetric load, query fans out). Connectivity servers store link graph compactly via gap encoding.
- Concept seeds: [[WebCrawler]], [[URLFrontier]], [[RobotsExclusionProtocol]], [[Sitemap]], [[Mercator]], [[ConnectivityServer]], [[TermPartitioning]], [[DocumentPartitioning]], [[Politeness]].
- Entity seeds: [[Heritrix]], [[InternetArchive]].

## [2026-05-23] ingest | IIR Ch. 21: Link Analysis

Source: [[iir-ch21-link-analysis]]
- Anchor text propagation: terms in an anchor pointing to page p are evidence about p (often higher-quality than p's own text). [[PageRank]] = stationary distribution of a teleporting random walk on the Web graph. Transition matrix P = (1−α)A + αE/N where A = row-normalized link matrix, E = all-ones (or teleport-to-topic for topic-sensitive), α ≈ 0.15. Solved by power iteration π_{t+1} = π_t P until convergence (ergodicity guarantees uniqueness).
- Topic-sensitive PageRank: per-topic teleport vectors, combined at query time by topic-classified query.
- Kleinberg's HITS: query-dependent root + base set; iterative h(v) = Σ_{(v,u)∈E} a(u), a(v) = Σ_{(u,v)∈E} h(u) with normalization. Hubs converge to principal eigenvector of AA^T, authorities of A^TA.
- Concept seeds: [[PageRank]], [[HITS]], [[HubsAndAuthorities]], [[MarkovChain]], [[StationaryDistribution]], [[Teleportation]], [[PowerIteration]], [[AnchorText]], [[TopicSpecificPageRank]], [[Ergodicity]].
- Entity seeds: [[LarryPage]], [[SergeyBrin]], [[JonKleinberg]].

## [2026-05-23] ingest | Designing ML Systems — Ch 2: Introduction to Machine Learning Systems Design

Source: [[dmls-ch02-intro-design]]

## [2026-05-23] ingest | Designing ML Systems — Ch 6: Model Development and Offline Evaluation

Source: [[dmls-ch06-model-development]]
- Six model-selection tips: avoid SOTA-trap, start with simplest, watch human biases, now-vs-later trade-offs, understand assumptions; [[FourPhasesOfMLDevelopment]] adoption arc.
- [[ModelEnsemble]]: 20-of-22 Kaggle 2021 winners used ensembles; 70%-classifier → 78.4% accuracy worked example; [[Bagging]] / [[Boosting]] / [[Stacking]] taxonomy; uncorrelated base learners principle.
- [[ExperimentTracking]] + [[Versioning]]: track loss curves, F1, gradient norms, weight norms, system metrics; data versioning is "like flossing"; CUDA atomic nondeterminism defeats bookkeeping.
- [[DistributedTraining]]: data-parallel (sync/async SGD, [[GradientStaleness]]), model-parallel (often serializes), pipeline-parallel (GPipe micro-batches); GPT-3 175B = 3.2M batch size.
- [[AutoML]]: soft (hyperparameter tuning, Melis 2018 — weak well-tuned beats strong fancy) vs hard ([[NeuralArchitectureSearch]] via RL/evolution; [[LearnedOptimizer]]).
- Offline evaluation suite: baselines ([[ZeroRuleBaseline]], [[HumanBaseline]], [[RandomBaseline]]), [[PerturbationTest]], [[InvarianceTest]], [[DirectionalExpectationTest]], [[ModelCalibration]] (Platt scaling, Steck 2018 Netflix calibrated recs), [[ConfidenceMeasurement]], [[DataSlicing]] + [[SimpsonsParadox]] (1986 kidney-stone, 1973 Berkeley admissions).

## [2026-05-23] ingest | Designing ML Systems — Ch 7: Model Deployment and Prediction Service

Source: [[dmls-ch07-model-deployment]]
- Four [[MLDeploymentMyths]]: one model, performance is stable, infrequent updates, scale doesn't matter. Algorithmia 2021: 41% of >25K-employee orgs run >100 models.
- Three prediction modes: [[BatchInference]] (precompute + retrieve), [[OnlineInference]] (synchronous, batch features), [[StreamingPrediction]] (online + streaming features). Grubhub counterexample: 2%-active users → batch is wasteful.
- Cloud vs [[EdgeComputing]] trade-offs (latency, privacy/GDPR, connectivity, cost). On-device frameworks: [[TensorFlowLite]], [[PyTorchMobile]].
- [[ModelCompression]] families: [[Quantization]] (Roblox BERT-on-CPU 7× latency, 8× throughput via FP32→INT8), [[Pruning]] ([[LotteryTicketHypothesis]]), [[KnowledgeDistillation]] ([[DistilBERT]]: 40%-smaller, 60%-faster, 97%-capability), [[LowRankFactorization]] ([[MobileNet]], [[SqueezeNet]] 50× fewer params, [[BinaryConnect]], [[XnorNet]]).
- ML compilers: framework × hardware N×M problem; [[IntermediateRepresentation]]s + lowering; [[OperatorFusion]] (vertical/horizontal CBR in TensorRT), [[LoopTiling]] hardware-dependence, [[Vectorization]], [[ParallelizationOptimization]]; [[AutoTVM]] beats cuDNN on ResNet-50/TITAN X after ~70 trials.
- ML-in-the-browser via [[WebAssembly]] (93% device support); [[ONNX]] / [[SavedModel]] export.

## [2026-05-23] ingest | Designing ML Systems — Ch 8: Data Distribution Shifts and Monitoring

Source: [[dmls-ch08-distribution-shifts-monitoring]]
- ML failure modes: software bugs (~80% per Google's 96-pipeline study by Papasian/Underwood) + ML-specific (production-data discrepancy, [[EdgeCase]] vs [[Outlier]], [[DegenerateFeedbackLoop]]).
- Formal taxonomy: P(X,Y) = P(Y|X)P(X) = P(X|Y)P(Y); [[CovariateShift]] (P(X) changes), [[LabelShift]] (P(Y) changes), [[ConceptShift]] (P(Y|X) changes). [[LabelSchemaChange]] and [[FeatureChange]] as bonus subtypes.
- Drift detection ladder: summary statistics → [[KolmogorovSmirnovTest]] (1-D only) → [[MaximumMeanDiscrepancy]] / Learned-Kernel MMD / [[LeastSquaresDensityDifference]] (multidimensional). Dimensionality reduction first. [[AlibiDetect]] callout.
- Adaptation: train on huge corpora, [[ImportanceWeighting]] (density-ratio reweighting), retraining ([[StatelessRetraining]] / [[StatefulTraining]]).
- Monitoring four artifacts: raw inputs → features → predictions → accuracy. Logs / dashboards / alerts ([[AlertFatigue]], [[Runbook]]s). [[observability]] ⊇ monitoring; ML observability also encompasses interpretability.
- Concept seeds: [[ServiceLevelObjective]], [[ServiceLevelAgreement]], [[TwoSampleTest]], [[DistributedTracing]], [[Telemetry]], [[PopularityBias]], [[DomainAdaptation]].
- Entity seeds: [[Deequ]], [[TensorFlowExtended]], [[TikTok]], [[YouTube]], [[GoogleTranslate]], [[Etsy]], [[PagerDuty]], [[Badoo]], [[DanielPapasian]], [[ToddUnderwood]].

## [2026-05-23] ingest | Designing ML Systems — Ch 9: Continual Learning and Test in Production

Source: [[dmls-ch09-continual-learning]]
- [[StatefulTraining]] (incremental fine-tune) vs [[StatelessRetraining]] (from scratch); Grubhub case: 45× compute reduction, 20% PTR lift.
- Four-stage continual-learning maturity: (1) manual stateless retraining, (2) automatic stateless retraining (scheduler-driven), (3) automatic stateful training (fine-tune from checkpoint, requires [[ModelLineage]]), (4) [[ContinualLearning]] (event-triggered updates).

## [2026-05-23] ingest | Designing Machine Learning Systems — book-level summary

All 11 chapters of *Designing Machine Learning Systems: An Iterative Process for Production-Ready Applications* (Chip Huyen; O'Reilly, May 2022; ISBN 978-1-098-10796-3) ingested via 11 parallel opus subagents — one chapter per agent on the pdftotext-layout-extracted text (markitdown lost heading structure). Source pages live at `wiki/sources/dmls-ch01-overview.md` through `wiki/sources/dmls-ch11-human-side.md` (≈ 215 KB combined).
- **Position in the wiki**: the **2022 predecessor** of [[ai-engineering-chip-huyen]] (2024), already ingested. Same author, broader pre-LLM scope (classical ML + DL production systems, not just foundation models). Where DMLS Ch 7 covers compression + compilers + browser deployment, AI Engineering Ch 9 deepens to LLM-specific inference; where DMLS Ch 9 covers continual learning + test-in-production, AI Engineering builds on that with LLM-era specifics. Refines/strengthens many existing wiki pages with the canonical 2022 framing (especially [[FeatureEngineering]], [[DataLeakage]], [[ClassImbalance]], [[ModelEnsemble]], [[DistributedTraining]], [[ModelCompression]], [[DistributionShift]], [[ContinualLearning]], [[MLOps]], [[ResponsibleAI]]).
- **Architectural through-line**: Ch 1-2 frame ML systems holistically (algorithm + data + interface + infra + ops; four requirements). Ch 3-6 cover pre-deployment (data engineering, training data, feature engineering, model development + offline eval). Ch 7-9 cover deployment + post-deployment (deployment service, distribution shifts + monitoring, continual learning + test-in-production). Ch 10 covers infrastructure/tooling (MLOps four-layer model). Ch 11 covers the human side (UX + team structure + Responsible AI). Order: 1, 2, **4-6, 7-9, 3, 10, 11** per Huyen's preface.
- **Concept seeds**: ~200 new concept wikilinks introduced across chapters (many unresolved — to be consolidated in a follow-up pass). High-impact new pages worth creating first: [[StatefulTraining]] / [[StatelessRetraining]], [[HashingTrick]], [[FeatureCrossing]], [[DataLeakage]] (currently stub), [[MLPlatform]], [[ModelStore]], [[FeatureStore]] (currently stub), [[ResponsibleAI]], [[ConsistencyAccuracyTradeoff]], [[SmoothFailing]], [[ContinuousColdStart]], [[MLDeploymentMyths]], [[InterleavingExperiments]], [[ContextualBandits]], [[ThompsonSampling]], [[DegenerateFeedbackLoop]], [[OfqualGradingAlgorithm]], [[StravaHeatmap]], [[ModelCard]], [[SubjectMatterExpert]], [[EndToEndDataScientist]].
- **Entity seeds**: ~80 new entity wikilinks. High-impact: [[Grubhub]], [[Coveo]], [[Faire]], [[ClaypotAI]] (Huyen's own startup), [[VilleTuulos]] (Metaflow), [[StefanKrawczyk]] (Stitch Fix), [[ErikBernhardsson]] (Better.com), [[JoshWills]], [[Ofqual]], [[Strava]], [[Roblox]], [[Dropbox]] (cloud repatriation), [[MichelangeloPlatform]] (Uber), [[Booking]], [[DanielPapasian]] + [[ToddUnderwood]] (Google ML reliability authors), [[ThorstenJoachims]] (interleaving + counterfactual eval), [[RonKohavi]] (A/B testing canon).
- **Contradictions / disambiguation**: no hard contradictions with the existing wiki. Soft tensions worth surfacing: (1) DMLS Ch 1's "latency = response time" overloads Kleppmann's stricter usage already in [[Latency]]; (2) DMLS Ch 2's "data is essential, for now" position predates the wiki's later [[ChinchillaScalingLaw]] / compute-optimal refinements; (3) DMLS Ch 5's [[Discretization]] uses "quantization" in the binning sense distinct from [[Quantization]]'s weight-precision sense; (4) DMLS Ch 6's "graduate student descent" framing has shifted by 2024 (AI Engineering updates this); (5) DMLS Ch 7's "online prediction is more expensive than batch" needs request-density qualification (Grubhub counterexample); (6) DMLS Ch 9 explicitly argues against "continuous learning" and "online learning" as synonyms — terminology hygiene note for [[ContinualLearning]]; (7) DMLS Ch 11 contains Huyen's own retraction of her 2020 "Kubernetes is essential for data scientists" position — propagate to [[Kubernetes]] / [[MLOps]].
- **Pending consolidation**: concept/entity pages were NOT created by the chapter agents (left as unresolved `[[wikilinks]]`) — a follow-up pass should stub the high-impact ones (the ~20 named above) and resolve case/spelling aliases (e.g., `[[Booking]]` vs existing entries, `[[Netflix]]` vs `[[NetflixPrize]]`, `[[Lyft]]` placement, [[ConceptDrift]] vs [[ConceptShift]]).

Sits beside [[hands-on-llm-ch01-introduction-to-llms|Hands-On LLMs]] (Alammar & Grootendorst 2024 — paid book) as the **free, official, code-runnable HF curriculum**. Coverage map: Chs 1–2 ≈ Transformer architecture + library API; Ch 3 = the canonical fine-tuning recipe (MRPC/GLUE); Ch 4 = Hub publishing + Model Cards (Mitchell et al. 2018); Ch 5 = Datasets library (Arrow / streaming / FAISS); Ch 6 = the **densest** chapter — Tokenizers library deep-dive (BPE/WordPiece/Unigram pedagogical implementations); Ch 7 = six task recipes (NER / MLM / translation / summarization / CLM-from-scratch / QA); Ch 8 = debugging + community engagement (the meta chapter); Ch 9 = Gradio demos; Ch 10 = Argilla curation; Chs 11–12 = the **modern LLM-era additions** (SFT+LoRA via TRL/PEFT; reasoning-RL via GRPO/DeepSeek-R1) — these two chapters didn't exist in the 2022 NLP-focused predecessor.
- **Architectural through-line**: introduce the [[Transformer]] (Ch 1) → use it via Auto* + pipeline (Ch 2) → fine-tune it (Ch 3) → share it (Ch 4) → feed it data (Ch 5) → train its tokenizer (Ch 6) → apply it to classical NLP tasks (Ch 7) → debug + ask for help (Ch 8) → demo it (Ch 9) → curate its training data (Ch 10) → instruction-tune via SFT+LoRA (Ch 11) → induce reasoning via RL (Ch 12). The progression mirrors the 2024 LLM-app stack from low-level architecture to production reasoning models.

The +7 lift fits the [[2604.14585-prompt-optimization-coin-flip|"can but doesn't" pattern]] — LM zero-shot defaults to extracting capitalized tokens regardless of person/non-person semantics; MIPROv2 installs the persons-only discrimination via instruction rewriting (the synthesized "regulatory compliance + public health communication" domain framing is a known [[MIPROv2|proposer hallucination]] that nonetheless optimizes the metric).

- **Scope-limit gaps**: tutorial does not benchmark [[BootstrapFewShot|`BootstrapFewShot`]] / [[BootstrapFewShotWithRandomSearch|BFRS]] as cheaper alternatives (the [[dspy-optimizers|page 13 rubric]] would suggest `BootstrapFewShot` for the 50-example training set); does not extract organizations / locations / miscellaneous entities; uses ordered-list exact match rather than span-level F1; does not characterize the cost-vs-quality Pareto across `auto="light"`/`"medium"`/`"heavy"`.

  4. **First DSPy receipt where the Signature docstring carries the persistence policy** — *"Whenever you answer a user's input, remember to store the information in memory so that you can use it later"*. Without this one sentence, the LM would only read from memory, never proactively write.

The framework refuses to fight the user's intent — consistent with [[DSPyModules|the Modules page's]] *"`forward()` is unconstrained Python"* discipline applied to async Python.

  1. **Async DSPy is not parallel DSPy.** The tutorial's *"sequentially but asynchronously"* comment pre-empts the common misconception. Consistent with [[DSPyModules]]'s framing that *"`forward()` is unconstrained Python"*: `aforward()` is unconstrained *async* Python, with the same hands-off framework discipline.
  2. **The notebook-runtime gotcha is the operational subtlety.** Jupyter / Colab cells run inside an existing event loop; `asyncio.run(main())` fails or misbehaves there but succeeds in `.py` scripts. Users encountering `RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop` in a notebook should know the tutorial's code is for `.py` scripts — fix is to `await main()` at the top of a cell, or `nest_asyncio.apply()`.
